author: Robert Philipson
title: Who killed the Shoga?
content:
The

shoga

 of the East African coast, a man accepted as a member of women’s society, did not emerge from a vacuum nor from the imposition of outside influence. She was born from the long encounter between Bantu-speaking Africans and Muslim traders from the Arabian Peninsula.

Unlike medieval Christianity, which not only condemned “Sodomites” but sought to prosecute and exterminate them, the posture of classical Islam was categorically different.

Liwat

 [anal intercourse between men] was prohibited, but in practice Islamic jurisprudence was less interested in policing private lives than its Christian counterpart. That was left to Allah’s judgment. Sin may have required repentance, but not necessarily prosecution.

This created a

de facto

 tolerance for discrete same-sex relationships throughout the Muslim world. And not always that discrete. The beloved youth — the

ghulam or amrad

 — appears throughout classical Arabic and Persian poetry, not as a scandalous figure but as a positively conventional object of male desire.

It is into this Islamic cultural framework, transplanted to the East African coast over centuries of trade, settlement, and intermarriage, that the figure of the

shoga

 first appears. The Swahili world was one in which Islam was constitutive — shaping law, poetry, architecture, commerce, and domestic life. Kiswahili reflects this: some 30 percent of its vocabulary derives directly from Arabic. To understand the

shoga

 is to understand how an Islamic cultural tolerance for gender difference was absorbed, transformed, and ultimately owned by the African women who gave the role its name.

Kiswahili-speaking women used the term

shoga

 [pl.

mashoga

], roughly equivalent to “girlfriend,” as a term of endearment. At some point this term was applied to Swahili men who dressed as women, performed women’s tasks, and were accepted into women’s society. It wasn’t the men who named and defined the

shoga

. It was the women. This makes any presumed Western equivalent inadequate or misleading.

Furthermore,

mashoga

 were recognized for the social roles they played and were not defined by same-sex desire, either coming from or directed toward them. How did the

shoga

 develop? How did she find her place in society? Written non-Western sources are silent on the subject. Early Arabic travelers and geographers wrote about commerce, politics, and religious practice, not about the interior arrangements of women’s domestic spaces. The

shoga

 was part of the women’s world — sometimes with special ritual or societal functions — smoothly and unproblematically integrated into the whole. What was there to say?

Plenty, once the Europeans started meddling in Swahili affairs. The judgments and pejorative terms followed in a predictable train.

Johann Krapf

, a German missionary working outside of Mombasa, compiled the first comprehensive Swahili dictionary, in which the secondary meanings of

shoga

 are defined as 1) a “catamite” [a boy kept for sexual purposes by an older man] or passive homosexual partner, and 2) an “impotent” or feminized male.

We see again the Western insistence on defining variant male gender identity not through integrated social roles but through sexual acts. When you only have a hammer, everything looks like a nail.

The hammer in this case was

Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code

, drafted by Thomas Babington Macaulay in 1860 for the British colonial administration. This punished “carnal intercourse against the order of nature” with up to life imprisonment. British administrators exported this provision to their African colonies without qualm —

more than half of the world’s remaining sodomy laws are relics of British colonial rule

, spanning 17 African countries.

Colonialism didn’t bring same-sex desire and gender variance to sub-Saharan Africa — the historical and anthropological evidence is irrefutable on that point — but it did introduce homophobia. Criminalized now,

mashoga

 had to go underground or into hiding. They were never in control of their own narrative, and generations of missionaries, anthropologists, administrators, and “observers” forced upon them whatever Western sexual-deviant theory was in vogue at the time.

And just when it seemed the

mashoga

 could be permanently dismissed, they were resuscitated and transformed beyond recognition by theories of essentialism imported from the gay liberation movements of the West. They were “born this way” and …

author: Glory Chidera Madueke
title: Nigeria Is Building an AI Economy. Who Will Protect Nigerians When the Algorithms Get It Wrong?
content:
By the time Nigeria puts together all of the policies needed to regulate artificial intelligence, elements of the technology might have already been implemented. In May, Nigeria’s federal government unveiled an open-access, multilingual voice and text assistant called

GovGuide Nigeria

, built by Publica AI with Nigeria’s Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, NCAIR and Meta. Its stated goal is to assist Nigerians in accessing government services in English, Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba.


A month later, in June, Communications Minister Bosun Tijani laid out the plan for a

National AI Trust

 that would guide the next phase of Nigeria’s AI adoption, investment and responsible innovation.


Meanwhile, Nigeria’s IT regulator, NITDA, has already put out an

AI Transformation Roadmap

 that extends much further than a simple chatbot. Among other proposals, it contemplates using ML to process documents, generative AI for preliminary drafts of regulatory texts, and “agentic AI” to manage and coordinate work across departments. This is a remarkable string of actions: Nigeria is putting its regulators in the stadium after its algorithmic players are already in the game. President Bola Tinubu aims to build a

$1 trillion economy by 2030

, and has looked to advancing technology to achieve faster public services, greater access to finance and higher productivity.


NITDA AI Hub, Lagos


Nigeria also has the necessary critical mass of users to leverage digital government, as evidenced by its over 100 million National Identity Numbers issued,

according to the World Bank

, and over eight million households supported through a national social safety net programme.


At that scale, these systems could become difficult to handle when failures spread across millions of people.


There is legal protection, but in practice, how effective is that right?

Section 37 of Nigeria’s Data Protection Act

 gives a data subject the right not to be subjected to a decision based solely on automated processing of personal data, including profiling, where that decision produces legal or similarly significant effects. Where an exception applies, the Act requires safeguards, including the right to obtain human intervention, express the data subject’s point of view and contest the decision.


Such a law provides an outstanding right.


In fact, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission reports in its

2024 Annual Report

 that many data controllers seem to disregard the requirement of a real human when making decisions, a practice the report describes as “quite notorious in credit scoring.” The Commission also says there is “a strong suspicion that many data subjects may have been refused certain benefits without knowing the real rationale for refusal.” Nigeria’s leadership would benefit from investigating this last observation. Nigeria will not gain public trust if it fails to ensure that its laws regarding these technologies are followed by private and public actors in the country. It also raises a practical question: what will constitute meaningful, rather than arbitrary, human review in automated decision-making?


Meaningful human intervention entails more than having a person oversee an automated process. When a government agency uses an AI model either produced or maintained by a third-party company, that agency must still have the means to examine the information needed to understand how the decision was reached and to find the root cause of an error. Otherwise, the government loses track of what is being decided and where errors arise. This affects more than determining responsibility; it is essential to the government’s own ability to maintain and improve systems.


Woman using a smartphone in Lagos, Nigeria


The companies with deeper pockets in the space, such as those developing the technologies Nigeria wants to purchase, may not always be able or willing to disclose how their systems work because of privacy, security or proprietary concerns. Nigeria’s government should not simply seek to be a user, but a smart user. Contracts with third-party developers should ensure government has access to inspect and understand AI systems, not give companies free rein to adjust their terms of service or data requirements without re-evaluation.


That makes

NITDA’s existing IT project-clearance role

 more relevant: public institutions are already required to obtain NITDA clearance for IT projects, a process designed in part …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Laws and Resurgent Cultural Claims: Rwanda’s Decency Policing Erodes Women’s Freedoms
content:
There’s been an online uproar after Rwandan National Police spokesperson ACP Rutikanga Boniface announced on public television that public indecency will be punished. On August 29, police officers threatened to beat young women attending a concert by Tanzanian singer Diamond Platnumz if they did not follow the new ‘decency’ orders.


In Rubavu, a town in the west of the country, a young woman was seen on video being apprehended by police over the length of her dress. Thereafter, several government workers using the X platform stated that it is important for Rwandan culture to be upheld and that the ‘Western ways’ used to sexualize women’s bodies through revealing clothing are corrupting the youth. These are not isolated incidents.


Women’s bodies and the rights of gender-expansive and marginalized people have increasingly become battlegrounds for Christian fundamentalist moralists and lobbyists.


Rwandan law does not clearly define indecency.

Article 143 of Law N° 68/2018 states: “Any person who performs an indecent act in public commits an offence.” Conviction can lead to imprisonment for six months to two years.

 In 2023, there were discussions about redefining indecency as “showing one’s private parts or performing sexual acts in public,” but this was not adopted. Ambiguity remains over what constitute

s a ‘private part,’ making enforcement unclear and subjective. This also opens the door to bias against women and girls, as body parts like shoulders or cleavage may be deemed indecent, similar to theocratic states treating exposed hair as indecent.


Social media is flooded with calls for clarity on the law, as its guidelines would be replicated at entrances to businesses, hotels, and restaurants. This demonstrates how legal ambiguity fuels public scrutiny and the policing of women and girls. Women are speaking up about how legal definitions of decency affect their lives. We cannot live in a world where a mere body can incriminate a person, or where enforcers arbitrarily decide what clothing is

 inappropriate

.


This debate is feeding into an already pervasive culture of gender-based violence whose victims are disproportionately women, girls and gender expansive people. Technology Facilitated Gender Based Violence (TFGBV), already common, is being fueled on TikTok and Instagram, where several young men and some journalists are justifying rape as the woman or girl’s fault due to what she is wearing.


On September 2, a young woman in Kibagabaga was harassed, beaten, undressed, and insulted by a group of men. The video has circulated on social media, but the perpetrators remain unpunished, and the girl’s fate is unknown. Now, online platforms—driven by manosphere communities and technocapitalists profiting from dehumanization—have become battlegrounds for controlling women’s public and private lives.


Mob violence and GBV have been normalized as of late, and public institutions have remained silent. Rwandan women and girls feel ignored, helpless, and abandoned.


The Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion, whose mandate is to champion gender equality, has in the past

 implicitly responded

to rising rates of teenage pregnancies by blaming parents and

mothers for failing to raise ‘decent’ girls

. Once again, the risk in this

rhetoric

is that women, girls, and gender-expansive people become blamed for such deeply rooted systems of inequality and oppression. Subjective matters such as manners, morals, hemline lengths, and even treating nudity as indecency are regressions rooted in colonial and religious control of African bodies.


Counting Women, Not Counting on Rights


All this is happening while women hold 64 percent of seats in parliament, yet they are not fighting against the resurgent social control of women’s bodies or the legal silences that enable it. Rwanda has had a parliamentary women’s majority for nearly two decades, yet this has not resulted in real change, as patriarchal control of women’s lives continues to resurface.


On August 7, 2022, police arrested 24-year-old Liliane Mugabekazi after a photo of her at a concert taken by a journalist circulated online. She was charged with public indecency under Article 143 and faced imprisonment. Prosecutors claimed her clothing “revealed her private parts”—her breasts. A Kicukiro Primary Court judge initially denied her bail. Mugabekazi pleaded not guilty, noting she did not take or share the photo and had passed venue security. She was later …

author: Christopher Rutledge
title: Free speech is not freedom from facts
content:
A strange thing happens to a claim when it moves from a WhatsApp group or a Facebook post into a radio studio. It changes its clothes.


What begins as a rumour on social media can sound very different once it enters a national broadcaster’s studio. The familiar presenter, the recognised station, the rituals of a professional interview, and the authority of being on air all lend the claim credibility it didn’t have before. The listener is no longer hearing merely what someone said online; they are hearing it through an institution they have been taught to trust, and it is easy to assume that if it has reached the microphone, someone must have checked whether it is true.


That is why the recent Broadcasting Complaints Commission of South Africa

(BCCSA) ruling against SAFM

 matters. It is also why some of the criticism of the ruling misses the point.


After SAFM broadcast the apology ordered by the BCCSA, some people asked whether organisations such as Macua (Mining Affected Communities United in Action) were now deciding what could and could not be said in the media. Others suggested that this amounted to controlling the narrative or restricting free speech.


It sounds like a reasonable concern. Nobody should want civil society, government, business or any political organisation to decide which opinions South Africans are permitted to hear.


But that is not what happened here.


We did not ask SAFM to stop interviewing Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, nor did we ask the broadcaster to ban March and March, nor did we ask that controversial views about immigration be removed from the public conversation.


What we were asking was fairly basic: if a claim is presented as fact, particularly on a national broadcaster, the audience is entitled to know what it rests on and whether it can be verified.


The lie about immigrants and crime


Ngobese-Zuma told SAFM listeners that foreign nationals were responsible for 60% of serious crime in Gauteng… Read that sentence again. Not that she believed migrants were contributing to crime. Not that immigration was, in her view, badly managed. She gave a figure: 60%.


A number sounds precise; it sounds researched and official. Once such a number is repeated on national radio, it begins to circulate.


People repeat it at work. Someone forwards it to a WhatsApp family group. A politician quotes it. A Facebook post appears, saying, ‘Even the radio said foreigners commit 60% of crime’.


Soon, nobody remembers where the figure began. They only remember the figure.


However, when the claim was examined, the evidence failed to support it.


GroundUp


and the

Institute for Security Studies

 investigated the broader claims about migrants and serious crime and found no evidence that foreign nationals account for anything approaching such a share of serious crime. Even the prison statistics commonly invoked in these debates do not tell the story people imagine: a significant proportion of foreign nationals in prison are there for immigration-related offences, not the violent crimes usually implied.


And this is the crucial point: saying that a police officer mentioned a figure does not magically make it a reliable statistic, especially since it has been debunked numerous times.


Anti-immigrant, ‘peaceful’ protesters in Alexandra, Johannesburg, carrying weapons and some covering their faces. File photo by Simon Ramapuputla


The BCCSA found that SAFM failed to inquire about the claim’s origins. The commissioner noted that the presenter neither endorsed the 60% claim nor challenged it, leaving listeners to accept it.


That is the distinction between censorship and journalism. Censorship says: you may not say that. Journalism says: you have said it; now show us why we should believe you.


The lie about foreign military bases


The distinction matters because the 60% claim was not the only one. Listeners were also told about foreign military bases allegedly operating in South Africa. They heard allegations that NGOs receiving foreign funding were buying weapons. There were claims that explosives were entering the country and that foreigners were paying police officers.


Again, these are not vague political opinions. Either the military bases exist or they do not. Either particular NGOs are buying weapons or they are not. Either there is evidence of a widespread system in which migrants bribe police officers or there is not.


When

GroundUp

 examined some of these claims, the picture began …

author: Dina A. Mohamed
title: Beyond useless guilt and insatiable victimhood
content:
In 2018, my first year living in Amsterdam, studying for a master’s degree in the arts, I went to a museum to attend a performance by a group of queer artists addressing questions of injustice. The setting seemed familiar enough until one of the presenters announced that anyone who did not belong to specified “marginalized identities” should leave the room. They began reading a list of those identities aloud.


For a moment, I just listened, suspended, trying to locate myself in the list. Then it became clear: the list excluded non-queer, white people. I, therefore, “belonged.” I found that the category I best fit in was “woman of color,” a definition I had never once used for myself at that time.


I stayed. The conversation turned to safety in the Netherlands, to harassment and violence connected to skin color, gender identity, sexual orientation. The others spoke from experience I could hear but not share. Amsterdam, for me, had been something else entirely: quiet nights walking alone through streets I did not know, a strange lightness I had no name for yet. No one had stopped me. No one had read me by my color. I am not denying that such violence exists, only that it had not, at that point, been my story.


And so, I said nothing.


That moment stayed with me. It crystallized something I had been sensing since arriving in Europe: a pressure, felt everywhere in public discourse, to read every experience through the lens of identity. To locate yourself on a map drawn by others and then speak only from that location.


What unsettled me was not the artists’ choice to create a protected space. It was the underlying logic, one I kept encountering: in seminar rooms, in cultural institutions, in the language of activist circles. A logic by which identity is constructed entirely on the axis of oppression: one group over another, history compressed into a single narrative, and every human being assigned a fixed position within it. You are either a victim or a perpetrator. There is no third position. The space between is simply erased. 


When pain becomes a pass


When being a victim is the only position that confers moral authority, the only place from which you are permitted to speak without being immediately questioned or condemned, then victimhood stops being a condition and starts becoming a currency. And currency, by nature, is something people reach for.


But to understand why this happens so readily today, you have to look at the broader cultural atmosphere in which identity politics operates. 


We live, as sociologist Frank Furedi argued in

Therapy Culture:


Cultivating Vulnerability in an Uncertain Age

(Routledge, 2004), in a society that has undergone a profound redefinition of what a person is.

 Clinical language such as trauma, triggers, nervous system dysregulation, safe spaces and emotional damage has migrated out of the therapy room and into everyday speech, political discourse and social media. The effect is that vulnerability has become the defining feature of how people understand themselves and others. To be a person, in this framework, is first and foremost to be at risk, to be potentially harmed, to be in need of recognition for your wounds. The self is constituted around its injuries.


This matters because it explains the ease with which therapeutic self-diagnosis feeds into political victimhood. When the culture already teaches you to understand yourself primarily through the prism of what has damaged you, and when the cultural framework simultaneously grants moral authority only to those who have been damaged, the two systems reinforce each other seamlessly. It offers people a coherent identity, a community, a moral position and a language, all at once. What it does not offer, and what it actively erodes, is agency. Therapeutic culture places people in a permanent state of recovery rather than transcendence: you are instructed to acknowledge your wounds endlessly and to identify yourself with and through them. Applied to politics, this means suffering becomes not something to be overcome collectively but, in a twisted way, something to be performed and preserved because it is the source of your standing.


Philosopher

Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò

 put it plainly: “pain — whether borne of oppression or not — is a poor teacher. Suffering is partial, short-sighted, and self-absorbed. We shouldn’t have a politics that expects different: oppression is not a prep school”. This is a difficult thing to …

author: WoMin
title: Wathint’ Abafazi, Wathint’ Imbokodo: Why Challenging Xenophobia Is Unfinished Women’s Business
content:
On 17 August, SADC leaders concluded their 46th summit in Durban, against a backdrop of heightened xenophobic protests, threats, and forced repatriations. August is Women’s Month in South Africa commemorating 70 years since women marched on the Union Buildings fighting against apartheid and pass laws. However, this month has been marred by the recent spate of Afrophobia and xenophobia across the country. SADC’s communiqué recorded an update from South Africa on migration governance and called for coordinated regional dialogue on the drivers of migration. It did not explicitly name xenophobia or Afrophobia — even after months in which Black African migrants have faced intimidation, violence, and pressure to leave South Africa. In an 

Open Letter

 to the SADC Heads of State and Government, WoMin African Alliance, together with The People’s Dialogue, calls for those Heads of State to place xenophobia and Afrophobia in South Africa on its formal agenda, issue a clear public resolution, and commit to measurable regional action. 


Those 20 000 courageous women across race, class and religion marched on 9 August 1956 to confront the Apartheid regime’s institutionalisation of white supremacy and racial capitalism by controlling Black life and movement. The Pass Laws inscribed that control, requiring pass books at all times, and described Black people as “aliens” and “illegal” in the country of their birth. Sophie De Bruyn, the only living leader at this year’s commemoration, shared “that the freedom we marched and bled for is in reality a painful paradox. How can we celebrate our past victories when our current realities are so deeply disappointing and distressful?”  


The pass laws did not simply restrict movement — they dictated who belonged where, who could work, where they could live, and who counted as fully human within South Africa’s borders.  


This historic day of protest was about fighting for a free, democratic South Africa in which all peoples, regardless of race, class and gender, could be emancipated and live with dignity and equality. Already liberated countries on the continent stood alongside Black South Africans in full solidarity, offering a home, bearing the brunt of economic pressure and military assault, especially for frontline states.  


While the pass laws are painful history, the current reality for Black South Africans falls far short of our freedom dreams. Much of Apartheid endures in lived memory — continued spatial injustice, the deepest economic inequality globally, and more than 33.6% unemployment. 


For WoMin African Alliance, rooted in Pan African feminist politics, this is no coincidence. Women’s Month cannot be commemorated as mere nostalgia — it must be treated as unfinished business. The emergence of Xenophobia and Afrophobia results from deep, intersecting crises in South Africa, as set out in our 

statement

 on Afrophobia and Xenophobia. 


The root cause of this crisis is the neoliberal economic policies implemented by the South African government, along with a long history of racial capitalism in which Black people were exploited for cheap labour to build the economy but have remained economically and politically excluded. What we are witnessing is the crumbling and disintegration of our society. Today, South Africa’s huge unemployment rate represents millions of lives suspended in a state of permanent insecurity. This disintegration has the greatest impact and consequences on Black women. 


Impacts on women

 


Women face the most inequality, earning 23% to 35% less than men for the same work, and accounted for 77% of all job losses in 2025. They are concentrated in low-income, informal, or precarious employment such as domestic work. Women-headed households face a roughly 60% chance of being poor. This places a triple burden on women, who bear most unpaid domestic work and child-rearing — labour unrecognised in national accounts and that hampers their economic advancement. 


These statistics represent structural violence rooted in inequality, patriarchy, social dislocation, and dispossession. Rather than confront the state’s failure to transform the economy and property relations, create decent work, or provide basic services, migrants become easy scapegoats for crises produced by capitalist and neoliberal policy. The unemployed South African is encouraged to blame the Zimbabwean street vendor, the Ethiopian spaza shop owner, or the Somali trader, instead of asking why …

author: Thandi Gamedze
title: Liberation Theology: The Unfinished Project?
content:
We live in a country in which white domination of black people is enforced with the use of teargas, the rubber bullet and buckshot during the day, and by hand grenades and petrol bombs, kidnappings and murders at night. We also worship—many of us—in churches wherein the same relations of white domination and ruthless brutalization of black Christians are reproduced. The unsuspecting black Christian believers are also dominated, brutalized and deformed theologically.


— Takatso Mofokeng


Writing in 1987, in the first edition of The Journal of Black Theology in South Africa (JBTSA), of which he was the editor, and at the peak of apartheid repression, Takatso Mofokeng poignantly depicted the context into which black theology in South Africa emerged, and to which it responded. Through its reappropriation of Christianity and the bible toward black liberation, black theology represents a resistance to the theological domination described. 


To this end, integral to black theology has been the appropriation of biblical imagery toward a faith that is liberating for the oppressed. The image of the crucified Christ is central. The suffering and oppression of black people are paralleled to the suffering and oppression of Jesus on the cross. This subverts dominant depoliticized and spiritualized views of the crucifixion, which invisibilize oppressor/oppressed dynamics and thus remove radical material implications for what it means to be Christian in a particular context. 


Equating Jesus’ torture with that of black peoples in a May 1993 JBTSA article titled “The Crucified and Permanent Crossbearing: a Christology for Comprehensive Liberation,” Mofokeng re-politicizes this story, reframing it as “a silent but visible indictment of humankind for lack of solidarity.” Similarly, in the journal’s May 1987 editorial, he compares Jesus’ tomb to material expressions of death of the time: “the crowded townships, squatter camps, shanty towns, migrant laborers’ dilapidated hostels and peasant shacks.” 


The Old Testament narrative of the Hebrew people’s freedom from enslavement is another that has been generative in the arc of liberation theologies across space and time. The JBTSA emerged in a context of severe theologically justified apartheid repression and aimed to create a platform for theological resistance to this. In its first edition’s editorial, Mofokeng describes the journal as “a forum for the exchange of theological ideas and a contribution to the development of Black Theology in South Africa and elsewhere.” In addition to Mofokeng, the journal’s editorial team included Simon Maimela (associate editor), and Itumeleng Mosala, Buti Tlhagale, Lebamang Sebidi, and Mokhethi Motlhabi (editorial board members). The JBTSA also had a range of contributing editors, including James Cone, Cornel West, and Jacqueline Grant.


Cone is often referred to as the father of black theology and published his first book, Black Theology and Black Power, in 1969. While South African black theology had its particular flavor, Cone’s work was influential. This generative relationship between South African and US black theology is illustrated in the first edition of the JBTSA which contains a report on the 1986 Black Theology Consultation in New York attended by eight South African theologians.


South African black theology was not only influenced by and influential to black theology in the US. It was also shaped significantly by other theological expressions, particularly that of Latin American liberation theology. This Latin American influence importantly brought deeper class recognition and analysis into South African black theology.


As black theology is necessarily always in dialogue with and shaped by its context, it is ever-evolving. In a 2009 journal article in Religion & Theology, Motlhabi, one of the editorial board members, charts the evolution of black theology in South Africa. In his framing, the final phase is characterized by “theological wilderness.” Motlhabi is unclear about whether this so-called wilderness is a “temporary lull in theological activity, a temporary retreat for the sake of more determined and permanent recovery, or the end (of black theology).” 


Although it could be argued that in the years since this was written, there has been a resurgence—albeit largely limited to the university space—in many ways black theology, along with the rest of the black consciousness movement, became largely marginalized within the …

author: Mahbub Abdillahi
title: Somalia’s uncertain hand-off
content:
This week, the Federal Government of Somalia held a domestic security conference in Mogadishu, attended by senior government officials and representatives of the international community. The conference came at a particularly critical time, as Somalia faces a growing dilemma on multiple fronts — the gradual drawdown of the AU mission in the country, the expected closure of international support structures, and an increasing political deadlock between the federal government and some federal member states.

These issues have been compounded by another concern that has grown over the past several months — the continuing threat posed by al-Shabaab and questions over whether the Somali National Army has the capacity to fill the

security vacuum

 that could emerge as African troops are reduced. However, the federal government is projecting far greater confidence in Somalia’s ability to manage the transition than many of its international partners anticipated.

Speaking at the conference, National Security Adviser to President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, Aweys Haji Yusuf, who is also regarded as an influential presidential ally, said the withdrawal of international missions from Somalia was “the result of a long-term process” rather than a sudden decision. He noted that discussions and “assessments of Somalia’s ability to take greater control” of its own affairs had been underway for more than four years. According to Aweys, the government sought to determine when Somalia would be able to reduce its dependence on the UN, with assessments concluding that Somali institutions were increasingly capable of managing political and governance responsibilities that had previously received substantial UN support.

Somalia’s Minister of Religious Affairs and Endowments, Mukhtar Robow, who previously served as a senior figure in the militant group al-Shabaab before defecting, also addressed the gathering. Robow said Somalia’s security environment had “changed significantly,” adding that the country was now in a stronger position than it was in previous years.

The comments come amid increasingly assertive statements from President Hassan Sheikh’s administration that Somalia is preparing to assume greater responsibility for its own security and governance. Speaking at the Hananbure military training centre in Galgaduud during the graduation of thousands of new Somali National Army recruits, President Hassan Sheikh said international partners had played an important role in supporting Somalia’s fight against a prolonged insurgency, but stressed that reliance on foreign forces could not continue indefinitely.

Somalia is entering one of the most consequential reductions in international support since outside powers began rebuilding the country’s security and political institutions more than two decades ago. Two processes are now unfolding simultaneously. The

United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS)

, the political mission that succeeded

UNSOM

, is due to cease operations on October 31, 2026, completing a two-year transition requested by the Somali government in the name of greater national ownership. Its responsibilities — including support for constitutional reform, elections, human rights, the rule of law, security-sector development, and the coordination of international assistance — are being transferred to Somali institutions, the UN Country Team, and other partners.

Separate from that process, however, is an increasingly acute crisis surrounding the nearly 12,000 African troops deployed under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM). Those forces depend heavily on the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) for much of the infrastructure that allows them to operate, including food, water, fuel, aviation, medical evacuation, communications, equipment support, and troop transportation. The convergence of the UN political mission’s closure with growing uncertainty over the future of this logistical system means Somalia could lose layers of international political and security support within months of each other, even as al-Shabaab retains a substantial presence across southern and central parts of the country.

The most serious shock has come from Washington. On July 1, Reuters

reported

, citing a US diplomatic note, that the Trump administration had informed the AU that it would no longer support UNSOS beyond the end of 2026 and would oppose a Security Council mandate continuing …

author: Siddharth Akali
title: Mineral Beneficiation: A Pipedream of Prosperity in an Unequal Financial Architecture
content:
Since 2023,

14 African countries

 have introduced

export restrictions

on unprocessed critical minerals, requiring “local beneficiation” – or in-country processing and manufacturing – prior to export, and demanding technology and financing.


Wealthier countries are also supporting the idea of local beneficiation and stepping up investments in resource-rich countries, promising this will help to lift them out of poverty. Behind these promises, however, they are perpetuating a top-down, economic model that only serves their own interests, and are reducing long-standing equity-based claims for climate justice and reparations from the Global South to a business opportunity.


Promoted by Western governments and executed through their development banks and corporations, this model pushes African countries further into debt, allows wealth to flow out through tax avoidance, and imposes policy changes that undermine environmental and human rights, while diverting scarce public resources away from hospitals, schools and social protection.


Geopolitical interests at stake


Currently, China is one of the world’s largest producers and suppliers of critical minerals,

controlling over 80 % of the rare earth element supply

. In response, Western nations in the

G7

 and their allies – who need to

secure access

 to minerals for their growing energy,

digital

 and

military

 industries – are trying to

reduce their dependency on China

 and stepping up investments in the mining sector across the Global South.


Amidst these geopolitical tensions, multilateral development banks (MDBs) are increasingly being used as a tool to advance Western government interests. In May 2026, the World Bank Group announced it “

will quintuple support to the sector in the next five years

”, while the African Development Bank is working to make

critical minerals beneficiation central to Africa’s industrialisation

.


Imider silver mine in Morocco. Credit Lorena Cotza


Development banks are mobilising support for mining and beneficiation in three main ways. Firstly, identifying and designing projects that can fit into global supply chains and are profitable for the private sector. Secondly, providing host governments loans to

absorb risks from the private sector

 through

public private partnerships

, and set up the associated energy and transportation infrastructure. Thirdly, under the guise of providing “technical assistance” as well as the conditionalities attached to loans, MDBs end up acting as

shadow governments

 and pressure African governments to make industry-friendly reforms, including measures to fast-track projects.


A promise based on false assumptions


MDBs are opportunistically presenting critical minerals as a golden development opportunity for Africa. Their promises of prosperity, however, are built on two faulty assumptions.


The first is that there is infinite demand for critical minerals. In reality, projected demand has been overblown, leading to overinvestment in production capacity. For example, global

manufacturing capacity for lithium-ion batteries

 is about two to five times greater than current demand, resulting in waste, overextraction, overproduction and lower prices. This suggests that mineral-rich countries will need to

increase demand domestically

, factoring in higher competition and reduced income for their products.


The second is that mineral-rich countries will be able to fund their essential social services and infrastructure through income from mining and beneficiation. However, debt servicing and the global tax framework (with business structures channelling profits to offshore investors) will likely suck up any economic value before reaching the marginalized communities who are facing poverty.


Unfair global tax and debt systems undermine public financing for development


MDBs have historically pushed for extractive industries to be

private sector-led

, leaving governments at the mercy of mega mining-corporations whose capital far exceeds the gross domestic product of many African countries. These corporations are pushing mining host governments

to compete with each other

 for more investments by reducing resource royalties, weakening environmental and social safeguards, and giving tax breaks to resource companies.


Significant portions of mining value continue to flow out as companies

shift their profits to tax havens

. Meanwhile the G7 and other wealthy countries

have …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: The “Rape Tournament”: Online Humour and Normalisation of Rape Culture in Namibia
content:
Between April 2024 and February 2025, Namibia recorded

 4,405 cases


of gender-based violence (GBV), of which 1,345 were cases of rape. These figures may not reflect the actual prevalence, as many incidents, particularly in rural communities, remain unreported due to persistent barriers to reporting. The most recent shocking case happened in June when a


25-year-old

 woman was gang raped at knife point by nine minors aged between 15 and 17. The news spread widely across social media, and with it came a violent


discourse

.

 One might expect that such dark and painful news would spark empathy, outrage, and solidarity. Instead, the news was met with many jokes, victim-blaming, sexual objectification, and open mockery of the survivor. These online comments are not merely insensitive humour. It is a disturbing display of how sexual violence is normalised and reveals social evidence of a broader rape culture in Namibia.


When Rape Becomes a “Tournament”


The title of this article emerged

from w

hat unfolded in the Facebook comment sections where the case, in effect, turned into a “rape tournament.”  At the dawn of the news, Namibians on Facebook rephrased this incident from a crime to sports, competition, and masculine camaraderie. In

this

Facebook discourse, the 9 suspects lined up in the photo like a football team, sparking sports references. A significant proportion of users, predominantly male, mocked the incident, curious about who the

“man of the match”

 was and who

“kicked the first penalty”.

 They further referred to the assault as a

“round-robin tournament,”

all of which transformed this violent crime into a public spectacle. 


This discourse appeared to erase the criminal and dehumanising act and reduced the survivor’s trauma to jokes and entertainment. Thus, the “rape tournament” term is used deliberately not to sensationalise the crime, but to describe how many commenters collectively reframed gang rape as though it were a sporting event. These comments construct an entirely different narrative about the survivor and perpetrators. She is no longer portrayed as a survivor of violence. She is rather signified as a playing field upon which the “match” occurred. This, in turn, frames the perpetrators as players whose acts are evaluated, celebrated, and compared. This shows that the football jokes were not isolated comments but formed a pattern.  


The social media comment section acts as a cultural space in which violence is publicly rehearsed, reinforced and legitimised.


The humour masked the true horror of the assault. When rape becomes a tournament, it sustains the rape culture in Namibia. Sexual violence alone does not sustain rape culture; it is also fed by the everyday attitudes, language, and habits that excuse, downplay, or normalise these acts. At its core, these Facebook comments show exactly how humour is used as a tool to keep rape culture alive and well in online spaces.


Victim Blaming Masked as Safety Concerns


Victim-blaming

 rarely appeared in explicit form. It was masked as “safety advice,” in which commenters framed their responses as concern for women’s safety. A significant number of people questioned why she was out that late at night,

with

one male user cautioning all women to stay indoors as soon as the streetlights go on to protect themselves. Women were advised not to walk at night, not to make unnecessary movements after dark

.

 One female commenter even suggested that the survivor should have remained at the home of the man she had allegedly visited and simply endured the “walk of shame” the following morning. At face value, these comments appear protective. However, they subtly relocate responsibility from those who commit violence to those who experience it. The discussion therefore ceases to ask why boys assaulted a woman and instead asks why a woman was outside.


The safety of women in Namibia is a concern given the increasing GBV-related cases in the country. However, the Facebook discussion extended beyond safety concerns and focused predominantly on regulating women’s movements, clothing, relationships and behaviour while remaining largely silent on the conduct of the alleged perpetrators. This kind of talk just aims to control women instead of questioning violent and toxic male behaviour. The burden of preventing sexual violence was therefore relocated from those who commit it to those who experience it. This sheds light on the double standards on …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: ‘Like ICE’: Western Cape police accused of unlawfully detaining foreign migrants
content:
Up to 200 foreign migrants have been in detained by the police since the 30

th

 of June as part of the state response to the anti-immigration protests led by March and March and Operation Dudula. The Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration declared even before the xenophobic deadline that the arrest of “illegal foreign nationals” would be intensified.


The Western Cape Coalition Against Xenophobia (WCC-AX) is raising the alarm over the conduct of the South African Police Service in Robertson and surrounding towns, which it likens to that of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE) of the United States of America. ICE is is carrying out the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign, often arresting migrants in public places and immigration offices. They have killed 8 immigrants and protesters this year, with over 50 detainees dying since 2025.


WCC-AX say that the rights of the migrants have been trampled upon as they languish in jail in Robertson and surrounding Winelands towns, denied medication, their basic sanitary requirements, and food. They are all from our neighbouring states, mostly Zimbabwe, and Malawi, Mozambique and Lesotho.


The Robertson police denied these claims and said food brought by relatives and supporters of the detainees has been allowed, but access has to be managed. “The station commander has confirmed that food brought by relatives is permitted, subject to a controlled process, and that visits are allowed but managed due to the large number of family members seeking access to detainees,” said the police.


But the police are not managing the acceptance of goods as it is arbitrary, with some police officers refusing and others being sympathetic to the plight of the detainees, WCC-AX responded. “The acceptance of goods,  including medication, has been totally arbitrary, with some police simply refusing to accept items, going so far as to say they ‘don’t care’, while other police have acknowledged this pattern and acted differently, but all entirely at their own discretion apparently.”


Sheriff Ramaobi, an activist in the area, confirmed that they were told that they cannot bring anything to the detainees. “One of our colleagues who visited one of the prison cells in Robertson asked these questions in terms of, can we bring medication or food supplies to our migrant brothers and sisters?  And it was denied. Other police stations, like McGregor and Montagu, strictly said that we’re not allowed. We are not allowed to give any support to the people that are incarcerated,” she said.


The police also deny that the detainees have been kept in jail illegally, saying that they have acted within the law and in cooperation with the Department of Home Affairs. “The foreign nationals detained for immigration-related purposes are dealt with in terms of the applicable legislation and in cooperation with the Department of Home Affairs, which is responsible for immigration administration and deportation processes,” said SAPS.


WCC-AX disputes this, saying that after they paid the admission-of-guilt fines, they were supposed to be released and not kept in jail for over two months. “If the police wanted to continue to detain them, they should have followed the administrative procedures laid down in s34 of the Immigration Act. The law states that people have to be told why they are being detained and what their rights are, including their right to challenge the deportation decision and to legal representation. Their continued detention must come before a court with them getting the opportunity to make representations. This did not happen. That’s why their continued detention is unlawful,” WCC-AX argues.


Anti-immigrant protesters outside the provincial legislature in Cape Town on the 30

th

 of June. File photo by Mzi Velapi


WCC-AX demands


The key demands of the Western Cape Coalition Against Xenophobia include the release of the detainees, for SAPS members to “stop acting like members of March and March (and ICE in the US)”, and act within the law.


The anti-xenophobia group is also calling for the suspension of police officers accused of failing to enforce the law and human rights violations, and that they must be subjected to an inquiry. The South African Human Rights Commission must also conduct an investigation. “The minister of home affairs must explain why his departmental officials conflate criminal and administrative proceedings in contravention of the Immigration Act,” …

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Federal government ends NunatuKavut’s bid for Indigenous rights
content:
The federal government has ended a years-long process to negotiate Indigenous rights and self-determination with the NunatuKavut Community Council, an organization that says it represents about 6,000 Inuit in southern and central Labrador.


According to a Tuesday statement from NunatuKavut, Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty informed the council in a letter on Sept. 4 that the federal government was terminating its Recognition of Indigenous Rights and Self-Determination negotiations.


“[

NunatuKavut Community Council]

 is a strong and modern Inuit government that remains committed to the recognition of our rights and the advancement of our people’s well-being,” the statement read.


The council said it was not given substantive reasons for the decision.


The federal government has reviewed submissions from NunatuKavut, historical and legal analysis, expert reviews and discussions with the council, said Jennifer Cooper, a spokesperson for Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada, in an email to Nunatsiaq News.


The evidence provided by NunatuKavut did not meet “court-established tests for Indigenous rights and title,” Cooper said.


She said her department has offered to meet with NunatuKavut to discuss its findings in detail.


NunatuKavut’s leaders have said

 its group’s members are of mixed ancestry who primarily come from communities south of Churchill River,

and are descendants of Inuit in the region.


They argue their members are the inheritors of a 1765 treaty between Inuit and the British Crown.


The group does not have a modern comprehensive land claim agreement, and the council has acknowledged that relatively few of its members speak Inuktitut.


The federal government has never recognized NunatuKavut as an Indigenous group capable of holding rights under Section 35 of the Constitution.


That changed in 2018, when Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Carolyn Bennett began talks with the group.


In September 2019, Canada and NunatuKavut signed a memorandum of understanding that recognized the group as an “Indigenous collective capable of holding section 35 Aboriginal rights.”


Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. welcomed last week’s reversal by the federal government, adding that

 discussions that involve Inuit rights, self-determination and governance must be in the

authority of “recognized Inuit rights holders.”


In a Sept. 8 statement on Facebook, Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami called NunatuKavut a “fraudulent collective,” adding such groups undermine Inuit and other Indigenous Peoples and can divert funding intended for Inuit.


The Labrador-based Nunatsiavut Government released a statement as well, saying NunatuKavut’s claims to Inuit identity are not recognized by Inuit or the Innu Nation.


“Inuit identity is not something that can be self-declared — it is affirmed by Inuit, grounded in our culture and history,” Nunatsiavut president Johannes Lampe said in the statement.


NunatuKavut maintains that it is “appalling that the minster of Crown-Indigenous relations would bend to pressure from other Indigenous groups on the denial of our claim.”


“We are Inuit. We come from Inuit. That will never change,” reads NunatuKavut’s Tuesday statement.

author: Dennis Ward
title: AFN investigating ‘incident’ involving Manitoba Regional Chief Willie Moore
content:
Willie Moore, the regional chief of Manitoba for the Assembly of First Nations, has been on a “temporary leave of absence” for the better part of the summer, APTN News has learned.


According to a statement from Andrew Bisson, the chief executive officer for the AFN, the organization “was made aware of the reported situation and has launched an independent investigation into the incident.”


“Upon completion of the investigation, the findings will be provided to the Executive and they will determine next steps. During the investigative period, the AFN Executive member being investigated is on a temporary leave of absence and their regional leadership has been informed. As the investigation is ongoing we cannot provide any further comment at this time.”


It’s not clear what incident Moore the AFN is talking about or the nature of the investigation.


Moore,

one of eleven regional chiefs

 at the AFN, currently holds four portfolios on the executive committee, including economic reconciliation and economic development, lands, territories and resources, social development and the management committee.


APTN has reached out to Moore for comment but has not heard back.


He was first elected to the role of regional chief in July 2024.


Prior to that, Moore was a councilor for Nisichawayasihk Cree Nation in northern Manitoba from 2014 to 2022.


The AFN is an organization that represents more than 600 First Nations across the country.


APTN has learned that Lake Manitoba First Nation Chief Cornell McLean has been filling the role as acting regional chief.


McLean declined to comment on the situation.

AFN investigating ‘incident’ involving Manitoba Regional Chief Willie Moore

author: Chris Walker
title: Ethics Complaint Filed Over Trump’s Cash Gifts to Natalie Harp, 3 Other Staffers
content:
The complaint alleges that there is a “legitimate question” whether Trump is paying staffers for their loyalty.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The Campaign Legal Center (CLC), a nonprofit whose stated aim is to defend democracy, has filed a formal complaint with the U.S. Office of Government Ethics (OGE) regarding monetary “gifts” from President Donald Trump to a handful of White House staffers.

Trump made payments of $45,000 each to Natalie Harp, his doting executive assistant who rarely leaves his side; Chamberlain Harris, his deputy director of Oval Office operations; and Margo Martin, a White House communications adviser. Trump also gifted $20,000 to Walt Nauta, his longtime aide and confidante, who was implicated in the Mar-a-Lago classified documents scandal before that case was dropped by the Department of Justice (DOJ) after Trump returned to office.

All four payments were disclosed on financial forms that federal employees are required to complete each year, with all of them listing the payments as “Cash Gift for Holidays.” Within the complaint, CLC specifically cited 18 U.S. Code Section 209, a law that prohibits executive branch salaries from being supplemented by other sources, including through the disbursement of cash gifts.

CLC also pointed out that these junior staffers were not eligible for the maximum salary given to White House employees. However, with the gifts, they reached that maximum salary figure of $195,200.

The organization notes that “preventing problematic gifts such as these is one of the reasons that Congress enacted Section 209.” Citing quotes from past court rulings regarding the law, CLC noted that, “After receiving a gift from a private source, ‘the employee may tend to favor his outside payor even though no direct pressure is put on him to do so.'”

“In paying White House employees funds beyond their government salaries, President Trump has created the same scenarios Congress specifically contemplated and sought to prevent,” the complaint from CLC said, adding that the payments raise “the legitimate question as to whether President Trump is paying [employees] for acting on his personal behalf, rather than in the interests of the public.”

The organization is demanding that OGE open an investigation into the payments and refer criminal charges to the DOJ, if the agency deems them proper.

As president, Trump would likely be immune from any charges, if the inquiry even gets that far. However, Section 209 doesn’t just prohibit the disbursement of outside funds for salaries, but also accepting those funds — meaning that Harp, Harris, Martin, and Nauta could potentially be indicted.

Kedric Payne, vice president, general counsel, and senior director for ethics at CLC, emphasized the need to investigate the payments in a press release accompanying the complaint.

“The American public has a right to know where government employees’ loyalties lie,” Payne said. “Laws prohibiting government employees from receiving supplemental income are not arbitrary; they exist to ensure that public servants’ priorities remain focused on public service, not a wealthy benefactor who may have other objectives in mind.”

“An investigation into this matter is clearly warranted, and, if a violation is indeed found, this matter must be referred to the Department of Justice,” Payne added.

author: Nora O’Malley, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: From beaver tails to seal ribs, new Ts’msyen cookbook spotlights coastal delicacies
content:
Rachel and Spencer Greening, with their child Maaya’ol, harvest seafood on the Pacific Northwest Coast. Troy Moth photo


This story was originally printed

in Ha-Shilth-Sa

 and appears here with permission and minor style edits.


Two Ts’msyen First Nations harvesters are putting traditional foods back on the table with a new Indigenous cookbook. 


PhD graduates Rachel and Spencer Greening devoted years of their lives to creating 

Gyetk: Coastal Fusion and Ancestral Knowledge from a Ts’msyen Kitchen

 (Gyetk is pronounced gy-e-tk and means “to feed the people”). It’s set to release on Sept. 22.


From maple-caramelized beaver tail over baked beans to roasted seal ribs with wild berry barbecue sauce, clam fritters and baked salmon heads, the Greenings’ cookbook features 60 seasonal recipes born from the Ts’msyen people of the Pacific Northwest Coast.   


“Up north, it’s a lot more common to trap beaver,” said Spencer.  


“Non-Indigenous and Indigenous folks who still do harvesting in that way will have beaver in their freezer.


“Some of these cuts of meats can be quite overlooked, even though they are nutritional powerhouses, and that’s why we highlighted specifically the beaver tail. Also, it’s really kind of comparable to pork belly.”


Rachel added: “I personally love baked fish heads. It’s a simple recipe.”


Old flavours in a modern world


Spencer, a storyteller, is an anthropologist whose research centers on Ts’msyen ecological knowledge, stewardship, and governance, while dabbling in archaeology. 


Rachel, a dietician, works in clinical and community dietetics and as a diabetes educator with Nuu-chah-nulth First Nations.


They regularly facilitate 

food-based workshops with First Nations Youth

 along the coast, emphasizing the role of harvesting in individual and collective well-being.


“We just hope people can see the intention behind the book,” said Spencer. “How do we re-empower these Indigenous palates? Palates have been colonized. So how do we massage these old flavours into a modern world?”


Rachel said it’s also about preserving knowledge.


“Because if we don’t preserve it, it’s going to be gone. We want it down in text, so people can remember and get excited.”


Rachel and Spencer Greening with their new cookbook Gyetk. Troy Moth photo


They kick off a six-week book tour with a sold-out launch party at the Clayoquot Campus in Tla-o-qui-aht First Nations territory (Tofino) on Sept. 22.


They have more stops scheduled across “Canada” in Nanaimo, “Victoria,” “Vancouver” (

Sept. 25

 and 

Sept. 26

), “Prince George,” “Prince Rupert,” Winnipeg and Toronto. They’ll also head to Seattle, the Gulf Islands and then up the coast to Haida Gwaii.


The duo will share complimentary food samples at most stops on the tour.


Celebrating different flavours, textures


Rachel says she’s excited to talk to people about eating different animal parts — like fish heads, venison tendons, moose hearts and mountain goat tongues. 


“(Elders) really used to like the gelatin and cartilage that aren’t really common in our food system anymore,” she said.  


“Part of it is people have been taught that those offcuts of animals are gross or dirty and we just prioritized the beautiful filets and discard all the rest.


“I get excited about talking to people about eating these different flavours and textures. They’re so nutritious and they’re also delicious and we used to celebrate them.”


Spencer’s favourite recipe happens to be one of the simplest. 


“One that comes to mind is salmonberries with seal grease,” he shared.


“Seal grease coats your entire mouth and holds the flavour of berries in longer. It just makes it a more delicious experience. Those little tricks blow my mind. It’s such a simple recipe, berries mixed with seal grease, when you have the knowledge that comes with it.”


Weaving in other key teachings


Throughout the book, Rachel and Spencer thoughtfully incorporate the 

Sm’alyga-x

 names of species, the endangered language of the Ts’msyen peoples, plus teachings on ethical harvest. 


“Indigenous communities have written a playbook of how to harvest in a sustainable way in these ecosystems,” said Spencer. “Through the plethora of things shared irresponsibly on social media, we just wanted to be a responsible voice.”


They also share ‘how to’ steps on jarring salmon, wild berry jam and making broth.

author: Mark Engler
title: 25 years after 9/11, how do we build a movement to stop endless wars?
content:
This article

25 years after 9/11, how do we build a movement to stop endless wars?

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, on the surface it may seem that American foreign policy has followed a course filled with continuity. A quarter century ago, the U.S. launched the “War on Terror” in response to 9/11. Today, Trump’s attacks on Iran have embroiled the country in another conflict in the Middle East.


Yet while the War on Terror gave rise to a disastrous wave of military intervention, it also produced a historic surge of antiwar activism, which played a critical role in discrediting “forever wars” across the political spectrum. Whereas the Iraq War began with 70 percent public approval, Trump’s war in Iran has been widely opposed from the beginning, with only around a third of Americans

currently in support

. 


Jeremy Varon, a historian at the New School for Social Research, recently released the

first definitive history

 of antiwar organizing against the War on Terror. His book is entitled “

Our Grief Is Not a Cry for War

.” I spoke with Varon to discuss the organizing that took place against the war in Iraq that started in 2003, the impact the movement had, and how that activism has been popularly remembered — or, too often, forgotten. 


We also discussed the prospects for antiwar organizing today, when Trump’s attacks on Iran are wildly unpopular, and yet we lack a movement that can be a mechanism for raising the political costs of interventionism. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.


There is a very common impression

 —

maybe the dominant impression of antiwar activism under George W. Bush

 —

that the movement was a failure because it did not stop the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003. I think that is a distorted perception of the impact the movement did have. What is your assessment?


The first thing to say is that success and failure are relative. And indeed, certainly with regard to the invasion of Iraq, the movement failed in its overarching goal to stop the war before it started. A lot of people intuitively knew that when the bombs started falling, disaster would follow, and that reorienting American policy would be like turning around a tanker, not a tugboat. 


If you look at American military casualties, the implosion of Iraqi society, civilian casualties and so on, the calamity that people feared came to pass. I can appreciate the sense of failure many activists felt, because the stakes were so high — literally life and death.


Previous Coverage


Lessons from the movement to stop the ‘war on terror’


That said, the antiwar movement can claim accomplishments as well. It substantially delegitimated the war before it ever started, especially within the realms of global public opinion and even geopolitics. The United States went to war with just one significant military and political ally: the United Kingdom. It didn’t have the support of traditional allies in Western Europe, like France and Germany. Most of Latin America, Asia and Central Europe rejected the U.S. position. The United Nations, while not declaring the war illegal, fundamentally disapproved of it, and Secretary General Kofi Annan privately thought the war would be a grave mistake. So the actual military campaign was inhibited by both a domestic and a global movement arguing that the war was wrong-headed and likely illegal. 


In a way, the antiwar movement peaked before the Iraq War even started. On February 15, 2003, you had thousands of coordinated antiwar protests all over the world. Between 15 and 30 million people turned out to protest the war. It was the largest single day of protest in human history. For sure, many people on the streets that day were gravely disappointed that the demonstration didn’t have the intended effect of preventing the war. Some percentage maybe never came back to the antiwar movement, because they were so dispirited. But organizing the mass demonstrations built a protest infrastructure that lived on. The main antiwar coalition in the U.S. came into its own through those demonstrations.


I give enormous credit to the people who had the tenacity and stamina to keep grinding away at protest. I’m thinking of Code Pink, United for Peace and Justice, World Can’t Wait and all of these smaller grassroots formations throughout the country that continued to organize.


When the war started, public opinion …

content:
C4SS

. Pubblicato l’otto settembre 2026 con il titolo

An Attack on Tech Freedom, an Assault on Dissent

. Traduzione di

Enrico Sanna

.


Viviamo in un mondo caratterizzato da

stato di polizia

,

militarizzazione della polizia

, e

repressione


del


dissenso

. Con i colossi aziendali spesso alleati con lo stato per

mettere a tacere chi dissente

 o per rafforzare la

sorveglianza

.


Dato il contesto, è importante che i gruppi autonomi abbiano piattaforme di comunicazione e hosting criptate.


Per aver fatto ciò, un collettivo italiano è stato recentemente

dichiarato

 “associazione terroristica globale” dall’amministrazione Trump. Il collettivo è Autistici/Inventati, che offre servizi ad attivisti tramite il servizio di hosting

NoBlogs

 e altre infrastrutture digitali.


Secondo

 il dipartimento di stato degli Stati Uniti, “Autistici/Inventati (A/I) è un gruppo estremista con base in Italia che crea e gestisce infrastrutture digitali al servizio di cellule antifasciste (antifa) violente e gruppi militanti di estrema sinistra in tutto il mondo”.


L’accento sulle

cellule antifasciste

 riflette il tentativo in corso dell’amministrazione Trump di abbattere il dissenso demonizzando gli “antifascisti”. Questo è l’obiettivo esplicito del memorandum presidenziale sulla sicurezza nazionale (

NSPM-7

), ed è alla base delle azioni penali contro gli attivisti anti-CIE (che gestisce i rimpatri), come

Minneapolis 15

 e

Prairieland defendants

.


Nel loro desiderio ossessivo di collegare tutto il dissenso anarchico e di sinistra agli “antifascisti”, l’amministrazione Trump è incorsa in dichiarazioni sfacciatamente false. Così il dipartimento di stato:


L’organizzazione antifascista Rose City, con base nell’Oregon, si è servita di strutture e servizi del collettivo A/I per coordinare e spingere a compiere localmente atti violenti e criminali, compreso un attacco contro gli elicotteri della polizia di frontiera che ha portato ad una denuncia federale. Rose City si è inoltre servita di strumenti e servizi di A/I per diffondere liste di proscrizione e informazioni personali ottenute illegalmente sulla polizia di frontiera, oltre a inviti a prendere di mira agenti in strada e “in casa loro”.


Ma come

fa notare

 la rete antifascista Torch, Rose City non è responsabile di tali azioni e non si serve di A/I. Gli agenti federali si riferiscono ai comunicati di Rose City Counter-Info, un’organizzazione completamente diversa che fa uso dei servizi di A/I. “Rose City” è un appellativo molto comune a Portland, nell’Oregon. Il nome accomuna organizzazioni diverse tra loro. Si tratta di chiare falsità ingenuamente amplificate da giornalisti di

Fox News

 e

National Review

.


Al di là dell’incompetenza dimostrata, dire che il collettivo A/I è una “associazione terroristica globale” è, questa sì, una minaccia serissima. Come

afferma

 il coordinatore tecnico di C4SS William Gillis, “È un FORTE attacco contro il diritto elementare di libertà di parola. Non oso immaginare quale colpo potrebbe subire un movimento anarchico costituito, come dicono gli Stati Uniti, da 5.500 mailing list e 10.000 blog.”


Il dipartimento di stato punta il dito contro gli utenti dei servizi di A/I accusandoli di aver commesso presunti reati, come il sabotaggio e il terrorismo. Ma si tratta perlopiù di attività che rientrano chiaramente nel primo emendamento (libertà di parola, religione, stampa e assemblea,

NdT

). Ci rientrano l’organizzazione di fiere del libro anarchico, attività di ricerca antifascista che studiano e denunciano organizzazioni di estrema destra e anche il blog di una rivista accademica di revisione paritaria e una trasmissione radio con podcast anarchico.


Classificare A/I come “associazione terroristica globale” significa a sanzioni. Significa che chiunque faccia transazioni con A/I si espone a rappresaglie legali, e questo sulla base di un decreto dell’esecutivo. Il risultato è che il sito del collettivo è stato

chiuso

,

PayPal

 ha bloccato il conto e lo stesso conta di fare l’italiana

Banca Etica

,


Si tratta di sanzioni che hanno un effetto devastante per A/I.

Così


Sabot Media

: “Il sei settembre, undici giorni dopo che gli Stati Uniti hanno messo il collettivo italiano nell’elenco delle attività terroristiche, A/I ha annunciato che chiuderà, tutti i servizi di email, blogging, hosting e comunicazioni offerti da venticinque anni saranno interrotti.”


Un precedente agghiacciante. Il governo può …
