author: Pip Hinman
title: Bob Brown: Australian government ‘culpable’ for climate disasters like Nepal
content:
Former Greens leader Bob Brown said Australia is “culpable” for the devastation in Nepal because it was not acting seriously on the dangers of carbon emissions changing the climate.

Australia is co-hosting the COP31 summit in November, along with Türkiye. Yet despite talking up climate action, Labor set about lowering expectations after it was first elected in 2022.

Green Left’s Alex Bainbridge spoke with former Greens leader Bob Brown about Labor’s refusal to take climate action seriously, even though it is a co-host of COP31.

What do you think of Labor’s approach to the climate emergency and does Australia deserve to be co-hosting COP31?

The symbolism of turning on Beetaloo in the wake of the Nepali avalanche disaster is very hard to ignore.

But this Labor government, much like the far-right alternatives, is captured by the corporate sector, including Woodside and BHP, selling off Australian’s rights for a secure future.

They won’t be the only culpable governments in Türkiye, however. Labor appears to be better than Pauline Hanson, but One Nation and Labor are both culpable of making climate change worse.

Federal Labor is set to debate the so-called “improved native forest management” method. Supporters claim it is going save some native forests. However, it allows state governments to earn carbon credits to then plough back into an already dodgy carbon trading system. Should saving forests be contingent on companies being able to buy carbon credits?

We’ve got more than 600 national parks in Australia, and world heritage areas, and they’ve all been set aside for the nation’s future because of their natural and cultural heritage values.

They were never set aside because of the dollars that could be made out of it.

But we’ve got a watershed moment; if Labor gets away with this, we have this new dynamic whereby future national parks will depend, to some degree or another, on whether the corporate sector can extract money as a result.

The NSW Chris Minns Labor government went to the last election in 2023 promising a great koala national park. It never put a condition on that, nor would it have, because polls showed that 80% of Labor voters wanted that park created and want koalas saved.

But, since the election, Minns has added a rider that you cannot have the koala park unless you agree to a scheme that measures the carbon absorbed by the saved forest and sells it to polluters as a cheap “offset”, so they can continue polluting. This way the polluting corporation can keep putting greenhouse gases into the atmosphere and make climate change worse.

We need to look at this through the lens of United Nations Secretary General António Guterres, who has repeatedly said the quickest and cheapest way to deal with climate change is to stop logging forests. This Minns manoeuvre destroys that advantage.

Energy minister Chris Bowen is once again criticising the Greens’ decision in 2009 to block the flawed carbon pollution reduction scheme (CPRS), which we called the “continue polluting regardless scheme”. There’s a lot of rewriting of that history. Looking back, were the Greens right to block the CPRS?

How do you respond to Labor’s argument that the decision set the climate movement back by a decade?

Bowen and Labor have a blind spot on the Julia Gillard years, when the Greens got Labor to put through the carbon pricing scheme in 2011, which was a world leader and really did make a difference because it almost instantly lowered greenhouse gases emissions for the first time in decades and lowered electricity prices.

The CPRS, which came two years before that, was flawed. It had been negotiated by then Prime Minister Kevin Rudd with the Coalition. It was only when the Coalition pulled out that they said, “Well, now the Greens have got to put it through.” The Greens said we’ll amend it and they said “No”.

Large sections of the Canberra press gallery have glossed over the real action that was needed to tackle climate change and which the Greens got two years later with Gillard. Our scheme was so effective that [former Coalition Prime Minister] Tony Abbott had to try to dismantle as much of it as he could.

Let me just go back to the CPRS. The Greens said it is simply feather bedding for multinational polluters and we are not going to pass it. The media said: “The Greens have had it. There’s five Greens in the parliament. They’re going to lose at the next election.”

At the next election, our vote went up by 50% and …

author: Mick Armstrong
title: FROM THE ARCHIVE—US imperialism (November 2002)
content:
Four weeks after the 9/11 attacks, the US invaded Afghanistan. By early 2002, the Bush administration began making the public case for invading Iraq, declaring the country part of an “axis of evil” with Iran and North Korea. Undersecretary of State John Bolton soon expanded the list to include Cuba, Libya and Syria. (The name “axis of resistance”, including Iran, Syria, Hezbollah and Hamas, was reportedly coined in response to all this.)

It became clear very quickly, however, that the analysis laid out in our 12 September editorial was substantially correct. In March 2022, Condoleezza Rice, then Bush’s national security adviser, admitted to the New Yorker’s Nicholas Lemann that, in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, she had asked senior national security staff to think about how to “capitalise on these opportunities”, which were “shifting the tectonic plates in international politics” to US advantage. “I really think this period is analogous to 1945 to 1947”, she said. “And it’s important to try to seize on that and position American interests and institutions and all of that before they harden again.”

It is obvious to more and more people that the [impending] US war on Iraq has got absolutely nothing to do with defending democracy or stopping “terrorism”, let alone with liberating the people of Iraq. It is a good old-fashioned imperialist war—like when the British sent in the gunboats to prove to the locals who was boss.

The September 11 terrorist attacks were a godsend for George Bush. They gave the US establishment carte blanche to accelerate military expenditure, crack down on dissent at home and to adopt a much more aggressive posture on the world stage.

Following hard on the heels of the Afghan war, the war on Iraq is just another step by the US ruling class to assert its military and economic dominance over global capitalism.

But why Iraq?

At one level it doesn’t matter all that much to the US who they attack. They are out to demonstrate that the US is the sole superpower that can assert its might right across the globe, and provided they are victorious, the Pentagon planners don’t care whether the next target is North Korea, Sudan, Colombia, Central Asia or Libya.

The strategists of Bush’s “war on terrorism” have spelt it out very clearly—they are planning permanent war, with the US military engaged in country after country. They want to establish a US armed presence in every corner of the globe and over the next decade they want to launch a first strike nuclear attack somewhere.

The US ruling class increasingly see the enormous military superiority they have over all their capitalist rivals as their key bargaining chip to shore up the profits of US multinationals and to force their economic competitors in Europe, Japan and China to make concessions to them in terms of opening up markets for US goods. Taking out Iraq will be a graphic illustration to all the other powers of the US’s willingness to resort to force to protect its interests.

There are of course additional factors. To start with—oil.

The Middle East has long been of central importance to US imperialism because of its enormous oil reserves—control over which is vital to the interests of all the advanced capitalist powers. By putting an upstart like Saddam Hussein in his place, not only does the US military defend the economic interests of its multinational oil companies, it also gives the US vital leverage over Japan and the European Union, which are more dependent on Middle Eastern oil than the US itself.

Partly it is settling scores with Saddam. The US backed Saddam’s brutal rise to power in Iraq to crush the powerful working-class movement there and to secure Western interests. They armed him to the teeth with chemical and biological weapons.

But then he got too big for his boots, and as with so many other US-backed dictators—Milosevic in Serbia, Noriega in Panama, the Taliban in Afghanistan—they moved to eliminate him.

The problem was that Saddam was more cunning than most; he managed to survive defeat in the Gulf War and has played fast and loose with the US for years. His defiance encourages other lesser powers to stand up to US hegemony.

This makes him a marked man whom Bush is determined to eliminate. Cutting Saddam down sends a message to every other US client state—don’t step out of line or you’re next.

The other reason that Iraq and Afghanistan are important to the US is China. The US establishment sees China as the rising …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Two fossil states, one public bill
content:
Australia digs fossil fuels; Türkiye burns them. One exports coal, the other imports it.

Then came Woodside — a nine-year liquefied natural gas (LNG) deal, signed weeks before COP31 was awarded to Antalya. Two states, one fossil fuel relationship, one climate summit.

The partnership shows how both governments talk about climate finance and what they refuse to name.

Australia is hosting a leaders’ summit in Fiji in October and then Tuvalu. Why Tuvalu? Because the island is sinking and it makes a ready-made stage. But county’s leaders are not coming — Germany, Mexico and South Korea are sending ministers instead. The Pacific Resilience Facility has a target of $500 million; only $172 million has been pledged.

Had COP31 been held in Kaurna Yerta/Adelaide, the bill could have reached $2 billion.

The summits in Dubai and Baku were funded by petrostates — fossil fuel companies paid for access. Now it is Türkiye’s turn.

The answer to who pays is buried in the COP31 hosting agreement, passed by the Turkish Grand National Assembly on July 30. It lists many cost items but attaches no estimated price to any — a blank cheque.

The total is estimated to have already exceeded half a billion dollars — surpassing the cost of the NATO Summit held in Ankara just weeks earlier, and COP31 (Conference of Parties for the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change) has not even begun.

This money will come from the public. But this is not what the “climate finance” conversation is about.

The tourism revenue from the summit will flow to the big hotels. Türkiye’s Minister of Culture and Tourism, Mehmet Ersoy, is the co-founder of ETS Tour, one of Türkiye’s largest tour operators and Voyage Hotels.

The agreement passed with barely a question asked. Only one party filed a dissenting note. Five deputies voted against, 22 abstained; 38 opposition deputies voted in favour, while 115 opposition deputies did not turn up to vote at all.

The pattern is familiar; a 2019 law exempting thermal power plants from pollution filters passed in the same near-silence — until we published the attendance records.

Parliament had chosen silence; the public named it and the president was forced to veto the law he had just been handed. What is being named this time is different: the absence of 115 deputies.

Climate change is a capital transfer built on fossil fuels. What we need is an end to the destructive system the public is financing, not more finance to work within it.

Türkiye spent US$727 billion on fossil fuel imports between 2003 and 2022. Even 10% of that figure would constitute a major source of climate finance. But that money is already spent — feeding the fossil fuel system.

Asphalt, concrete, roads, buildings are fossil fuel systems too.

COP31 will be held on land built over farmland for the EXPO 2016 fair — used once then left idle — with a 150,000 square metre asphalt car park added for the occasion. They just are not named as climate policy.

The foundations of Türkiye’s largest climate-changing corporations came together in June to launch the “Philanthropy for Climate” initiative.

Who are the founding signatories? Koç Holding, which operates Türkiye’s largest oil refinery, Sabancı Holding, which owns Enerjisa’s coal and gas plants and Çimsa cement operations is a key player and TAV Airports, which operates Antalya Airport in the city hosting COP31.

They claim to be “taking responsibility for the climate”, but laundering it is a more accurate description.

What makes it worse is that environmental organisations, education and health bodies have signed on.

Sixteen organisations in Türkiye pushed back saying: “Those who are changing the climate cannot clear their own name”.

Other ecology and environment movements had no position. That silence gave Philanthropy for Climate exactly what it needed: civil society legitimacy.

“Climate finance” may be the most content-free phrase in the climate debate. Türkiye received billions of dollars of climate finance from the World Bank, among others, and its emissions kept rising.

The public money going to fossil fuel imports is another form of financing, but it will not appear on the agenda of climate negotiations.

A climate activist flying in from Australia for COP31 will land at TAV’s airport, stay in a hotel built by the minister’s company and sit in rooms where the “finance” being discussed will be none of the above.

This is not a COP problem; it is proof of exactly what COP is …

author: Tom Bramble
title: FROM THE ARCHIVE—War abroad and repression at home (November 2005)
content:
This is an edited version of an article written in response to the 2005 Anti-Terrorism Bill, which was rammed through parliament by Prime Minister John Howard’s Coalition government with the support of the Labor Party the following month (December 2005). 

The legislation gave security agencies the power to detain and question suspects for up to fourteen days without charge; and it made it a crime for people who had been detained to tell anyone about it. It also gave police the power to impose control orders on suspects for up to a year. 

Further, it reintroduced the crimes of “sedition” and “seditious intention”. The latter includes the crimes of intending “to bring the sovereign [the federal government] into hatred or contempt” or to “urge disaffection” against the constitution, the government or the parliament. 

Bramble noted that “the Australian government has passed 26 laws that restrict civil rights in the name of ‘combating terrorism’”. By 2021, the

Australian Financial Review

 could report that “more than 130 pieces of national security legislation” had been enacted since 9/11.

Howard’s latest “anti-terrorism” laws, due to take effect by the end of this year, are a drastic attack on the civil rights of all ordinary Australians and Muslims in particular. These laws are the direct product of September 11, but not in the way that our government would have us believe. 

Wars do not involve just military forces but ideological warfare as well. The enemy has to be demonised—to be rendered sub-human in order to justify its slaughter. In addition, an “enemy within” has to be created to cement “national unity” at home. 

Thousands of Muslim residents of the USA, UK and Australia have been subject to police harassment, detention without trial, secret hearings, censorship and torture. Their homes have been raided, their communications intercepted, and infiltrators and provocateurs planted in their communities. At the same time, the climate of anti-Muslim racism stoked by the “war on terror” has resulted in an increase in harassment on the streets, with Muslims being abused and assaulted.

Since 9/11, the Australian government has passed 26 laws that restrict civil rights in the name of “combating terrorism”. Howard’s new laws represent the further acceleration of state repression. Their purpose is not to keep us safe on public transport but to foster a climate of fear, suspicion and racism, the better to keep us divided. Such an environment helps Howard push through his unpopular agenda at home of union-busting, locking up refugees, privatisation of Telstra and the destruction of Medicare.

Under these new laws, Muslims in particular will be subject to control orders which allow people deemed in secret court hearings to be “terrorist risks” to be electronically tagged. Those subject to control orders will be subject for 12 months to travel bans, restrictions on whom they can meet, and bans on communicating with associates by telephone, internet or email. The government has already announced that it has its eye on 800 Muslim suspects

The legal tradition of

habeas corpus

, whereby people cannot be held unless charged with an offence, will be trashed. Preventative detention allows the police and ASIO to secretly lock up people for up to 48 hours and, with the assistance of state police, up to 14 days. Preventative detention applies not to people who have allegedly committed an offence or even alleged to have any information in relation to an offence, but merely on suspicion of what they may do in future.

It will be a crime for an organisation to “advocate” terrorism, which includes “directly or indirectly counselling or urging” a terrorist act, or “directly praising” terrorism. The range of groups that can be banned as terrorist will be dramatically widened and any of their members, supporters or financial donors can be imprisoned for years.

In order to push all of this through, the AFP and ASIO are undergoing a massive expansion, with ASIO growing from 584 officers in 2001 to 1860 by 2010. With this expansion in numbers goes ever-increasing powers: use of CCTV surveillance, the power to secretly enter and search premises, intercept communication and seize material. The AFP will have new powers to stop, question and search people on the street, seize documents and obtain airline passenger information.

The Vietnam Syndrome

The “war on terror” has a second major purpose: to overcome once and for all the Vietnam …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Nepal disaster a climate warning for COP31
content:
The disaster in Nepal, Tibet and China has been described as being like a “horror movie” — even by those in the midst of the catastrophe.

Just as the wildfires in Europe and the Black Summer bushfires in Australia, it is hard to imagine just how catastrophic these climate-fuelled events can be — until they happen — and even then, it is hard to get one’s head around.

But climate scientists have warned for decades that in an increasingly warming world — the result of human-induced activity — catastrophic events are hard to predict but they will happen.

Scientists have also warned for decades that tipping points — critical limits in the Earthʼs climate and planetary sub-systems (rainforests and ice sheets) where small additional changes can trigger major and potentially irreversible shifts that continue on their own — will be more frequent.

They have also pointed out the injustice associated with these disasters: countries that had the least to do with the problem are the worst affected. This is what we are seeing in Nepal.

The climate emergency — seen today in fires across Europe, the melting glaciers in the Himalayas and the developing El Niño in the Southern Ocean — is not new. But it is getting worse. Just as shocking as the catastrophic events themselves, is that those in power refuse to do anything to avert it.

This is where we need more focus. Once, the Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese told us that the climate emergency was the “greatest moral issue of our time”. Now, asked by reporters if the world has to take some collective responsibility for not doing enough on climate change, he said that “now’s the time … to focus … very much on people who are incredibly traumatised”.

The most useful way Australia could reassure people who are traumatised is by taking a proactive approach to this global problem, to which this country, a major coal and gas exporter, makes a significant contribution.

Albanese and several other ministers in Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum last week were keen to play down climate in favour of “security”, including the Pacific Policing initiative, which involves Australia training new recruits to counter “transnational crime”. But the climate crisis is the most serious transnational crime of them all.

Even Palauan President Surangel Whipps, not renown for being outspoken on climate, said: “It is hard to overstate the depth of emotion for those of us living on the frontline after having fought so hard to put the 1.5 degree limit at the heart of the Paris Agreement … calls for greater ambition are no longer enough — we need to see an urgent and unprecedented increase in political will and investment in a climate safe future.”

A United Nations Environment Program report, released in September, warns that global temperature rise is set to cross 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels by 2030. “There are no good outcomes in remaining above 1.5°C,” it said.

It said “potential tipping points” include irreversible changes to ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (the system of ocean currents that acts as a global conveyor belt carrying warm surface water north and cold deep water south) and the erasure of the Amazon rainforest. All these would lead to intensified extreme weather, ecosystem loss and submersion of small island states and low-lying coastal cities.

It said warming up to or less than 3°C would mean glaciers could lose more than a quarter of their mass by 2100 and sea levels would rise by 12.5 centimetres. Apart from severe damage to human health, food security, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies, it would mean “crossing thresholds that become difficult or impossible to reverse on human timescales”.

There is debate among climate scientists, some of whom say the UN is underplaying the scale of the global warming disaster. Climate Brink said: “Most forecasts predict that 2027 will set records, with the global average temperature reaching levels we would not expect until the late 2030s”.

The Nepal disaster is a reminder that climate change is the greatest security threat of our time. Burning of fossil fuels, which leads to more trapped greenhouse gases, continues to contribute to the accumulation of energy in the Earth system that, in turn, leads to uninhabitable temperatures.

Australia, a co-host of the COP31 in Türkiye, will argue that it is on track to reach its 2030 target of cutting emissions by 43% below 2005 levels …

author: Liz Walsh
title: FROM THE ARCHIVE—‘End this disgusting war’: an interview with Malalai Joya (November 2010)
content:
Afghanistan was supposed to be “the good war”—the war to catch Osama bin Laden, to liberate the women suffering under the Taliban regime, to bring democracy and rights to the population. It was all lies. The Washington Post reported in October 2001, on the eighth day of the invasion, that the Taliban was offering to turn over bin Laden to a neutral third country to end the US invasion. But the US government rejected the offer. 

Moreover, none of the 9/11 terrorists was Afghan; most were Saudi nationals, including bin Laden. But that country was a key US ally. The elections in Afghanistan, when they came, were a sham. And the country’s women were pawns in a US imperial plan to tear through the Middle East—the Americans moved on to Iraq in no time. 

One of the loudest voices of resistance to both US imperialism and the old and emerging Afghan “order” was Malalai Joya. She sat down with Socialist Alternative’s Liz Walsh in 2010, nine years after the beginning of the invasion and occupation of her country.

For nine long years, the United States and its allies have been tearing apart Afghanistan. And still their occupation grinds on. Few Afghan voices have emerged in condemnation of this barbarous war as forcefully as Malalai Joya’s.

Joya emerged on the international stage as a fierce anti-war figure and fighter for women’s rights when she was elected in 2003 to the 

Loya Jirga

, which was convened to ratify Afghanistan’s constitution. It was here that she used her 

maiden speech

 to launch a blistering attack on the warlords present at the gathering.

Joya was elected to the Afghan parliament in 2005, which she used as a platform to continue her courageous denunciation of all who oppress the Afghan people, from Karzai’s corrupt puppet regime to the Taliban insurgency 

and

 the occupation forces.

In 2007, Joya was permanently expelled from the Afghan parliament. Not surprisingly, there have been no words of protest at this attack on democracy from the occupying powers.

Since her expulsion, Joya has travelled the world to bring the truth of the occupation to Western audiences. She is currently on a speaking tour in Australia, where she has addressed refugee rallies, anti-war vigils and university lecture halls. Willing to speak to whoever will listen, Joya found the time to speak with me about her political activism, views on the occupation and hopes for the future.

Joya was not always a political activist. “At first I was a social activist. I didn’t want to be a politician.” For much of the 1990s, while Afghanistan was ruled by the Taliban, Joya worked with the Organisation for Promoting Afghan Women’s Capabilities (OPAWC) to set up underground schools, teaching literacy to girls and adult women.

She herself was educated in a school run by the 

Revolutionary Association of Women of Afghanistan

 (RAWA), while her family lived in a refugee camp in Pakistan, having been forced into exile by the 1979 Soviet invasion. It was here that Joya developed her staunch commitment to the importance of education for girls and women’s rights.

But in the aftermath of the 2001 invasion—faced with a mounting civilian death toll from the American warplanes that rained cluster bombs and white phosphorus from the sky, and a corrupt government filled with the very people responsible for terrorising and pillaging Afghanistan during the vicious civil war that erupted in the 1990s—Joya decided that she needed to intervene politically:

“When I was a social activist, I talked a lot with the people. I loved with them. I cried with them. I heard a lot about their stories, about the crimes these criminals committed against them. In 2003, I decided I couldn’t tolerate it anymore.”

But then she quips, “In the parliament they couldn’t tolerate me”.

Joya argues without hesitation for the troops to get out of Afghanistan:

“The troops only double our misery. We are crushed between two enemies, the warlords and Taliban on one side. They both continue their fascism. And the occupation forces on the other side. They are bombing and doing massacres. In my province, Farah, in one day they killed 150 civilians through bombs.

“It would be much easier for us to fight one enemy than to have to fight two. The occupation gives more money and more guns to these warlords. They are getting more powerful.”

She points out that the Australian government too has been directly aiding the warlords, with 

recent revelations in the media

 that senior …

author: Hend Salama Abo Helow
title: Widespread Poverty in Gaza Is Forcing Children to Become Breadwinners
content:
“Here I am, thousands of miles away from my dreams,” said one 14-year-old.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Despite the restrictions that had long stifled Gaza prior to October 7, 2023, it was a remarkably young society, shaped by high fertility rates and a culture in which raising children and building close-knit families were at the heart of life. Nearly half of Gaza’s population was children under the age of 18, who had been denied the chance to witness a normal, peaceful life.

Since the genocide began, Gaza has witnessed one of the deadliest assaults in modern history. Israeli forces have killed, injured, detained, tortured, and starved children, depriving them of their basic rights to education, adequate health care, and a safe childhood, as the United Nations’ Independent Commission of Inquiry has documented. Over the last nearly 3 years, children have accounted for nearly 30 percent of Gaza’s death toll, amounting to at least 21,000 victims. More than 44,000 have been injured, many with potentially life-changing injuries. Another 17,000 children have been left grieving the loss of their parents.

The UN Commission also found that Israeli atrocities amounted to genocide, crimes against humanity, and grave violations of international law. Yet, since the so-called ceasefire took effect, the bombs may have slowed, but they never stopped. More than 300 children have been killed since October 10, 2025.

As the Commission has stated, “the essence of childhood has been destroyed” by Israel. But the human cost extends beyond the staggering numbers of deaths: It includes the suffering of the children who have survived. They are being forced out of childhood, bearing burdens far beyond their age, and working to keep their destitute families afloat.

Ahmed Al-Nabahin, a 14-year-old child who should be in secondary school rather than shouldering the responsibilities of a breadwinner, is working as a wood and rubbish collector as a matter of survival.

“I was forced to drop out of school in order to keep my family of six afloat, as living expenses were skyrocketing,” Ahmed told Truthout.

Sweat streaming down his face, he told me that he usually kicks off work at 6 a.m. and returns at 9 p.m. “Exhaustion does little to convey what I feel at the end of the day, all for 25 shekels [almost $5 USD] in compensation,” he said.

Given Gaza’s depressed economy, no job lasts long, forcing Ahmed to shift between multiple hazardous jobs. He vividly recalled a moment when Israeli forces nearly took his life during a shift: “I was rummaging through rubbish in [the neighborhood of] Al-Zahra when a quadcopter attacked us.”

Ahmed sobbed, then continued: “I managed to escape by a miracle, but my friend was injured and bled to death.”

He added, “Each time I go to work, I know deep down that I am jeopardizing my life and may never return. But my younger siblings and mother are waiting for me to bring them food.”

As we spoke, a group of young children were playing football nearby. Ahmed tilted his head toward them. With a quivering voice, he said, “I wish I could play like them. I wish I could stop working and return to school.”

Breaking into tears, he continued, “I’ve been dreaming of becoming a prominent, talented football player and a dentist. But here I am, thousands of miles away from my dreams.”

Yet it is even more heart-wrenching for parents to witness their child paying the highest price. For Nisreen Abu Mallouh, Ahmed’s mother, the fear of losing her son has become a nightmare she lives with every day. She worries that Ahmed may accidentally cross the “yellow line,” the boundary of occupation demarcated by the so-called ceasefire, which is ill-defined and coming under more Israeli control by the day. “This specter keeps haunting me: maybe my son will be killed by Israeli forces or Israeli-backed gangs.”

His family had no choice but to accept the grave reality. His mother lamented: “Ahmed was an intelligent student, yet harsh life conditions forced him to … venture out to work.”

She added: “He has become more aggressive and angry, and his sleep has become disturbed since he started working. I feel he’s not Ahmed. He’s not the same Ahmed he was before the genocide.”

author: CMI Argentina
title: Cupo laboral trans: la Justicia ordena reincorporar a otra trabajadora despedida
content:
Los fallos exigen que el gobierno incorpore a trabajadorxs trans que habían ingresado al Estado por la ley de cupo laboral. Los casos que faltan.


Por Agustina Ramos. Edición: Maby Sosa


La Justicia ordenó la reincorporación de Natasha Narmona a su puesto laboral en el Ministerio de Economía de la Nación. Se trata de la primera mujer trans que ingresó a trabajar en esta cartera a través de la

Ley de Cupo Laboral Travesti Trans

 y

en noviembre del 2025 fue despedida

. El fallo favorable se suma a otros en el mismo sentido. Sin embargo, aún no fue reincorporada. Mientras tanto, otras personas travestis y trans continúan en engorrosos procesos judiciales.


“Esto no es un privilegio, es parte de la defensa de mis derechos y de mi trabajo. Es importante que el Estado no solo habilite el ingreso, sino que garantice la permanencia”, compartió a Presentes Narmona.


La sentencia fue firmada por los jueces Gabriel de Vedia y Enrique Catani de la Sala V de la Cámara Nacional de Apelaciones del Trabajo el 7 de agosto pasado. En ella resolvieron revocar la resolución dictada en primera instancia y hacer lugar a la medida solicitada por Narmona. En este sentido, ordenaron “la reinstalación provisoria de la Sra. Natasha Narmona en su puesto de trabajo en las mismas condiciones en las cuales se encontraba (…) dentro del plazo de cinco días de notificada la sentencia”.


Para la mujer trans despedida se trata de “una victoria colectiva”. Sin embargo, también compartió que el plazo fijado por el Poder Judicial para su reincorporación terminó y no hubo respuesta alguna de parte del Ministerio de Economía.


“El viernes pasado enviamos un telegrama denunciando este incumplimiento e intimando a que lo cumplieran en 24 horas. Pero ese tiempo también pasó y el ministerio no solo no lo hace, sino que tampoco explica por qué no lo hace. Esto es muy grave”, agregó.


Natasha muestra el fallo de la Justicia.


La lucha colectiva y la urgencia particular


El caso tiene una relevancia colectiva: implica la falta de cumplimiento de una ley

(la N° 27.636

) y de una orden judicial por parte de un organismo del Estado Nacional. En este sentido, el caso cuenta con el apoyo de un amicus curiae, una presentación mediante la cual organizaciones y personas con experiencia en una problemática pueden aportar al tribunal argumentos y una perspectiva de derechos. Son parte del amicus las organizaciones

ATTTA

,

ATE

,

Mocha Celis

, el

Movimiento Travesti Trans Argentina

 y referentas del colectivo como Pía Ceballos, Sher Lescano y Alba Rueda.


Desde el despido casi un año atrás, las condiciones de vida de Natasha empeoraron drásticamente. “Mi sueldo era el mínimo. Si bien no me alcanzaba –eran 400 mil pesos– me ayudaba a sostener de alguna manera mi vida. De poder tener un plato de comida, ahora dependo de un comedor que queda acá en Munro (provincia de Buenos Aires). Comemos mi vieja y yo. Yo soy cuidadora de mi mamá que cobra la mínima de la jubilación”.


También impactó en su salud. “Tengo un tratamiento psicoterapéutico y cuando me despidieron perdí la obra social. Hoy la salud pública está en una situación grave y esto me revictimiza. En el momento de mi despido además cursaba una fractura de peroné. Recién me operaron el 29 de julio”.


Natasha ingresó a trabajar al Ministerio de Economía de la Nación en octubre de 2021 bajo el marco de la

Ley de Promoción del Acceso al Empleo Formal para Personas Travestis, Transexuales y Transgénero “Diana Sacayán – Lohana Berkins” (N° 27.636)

. La normativa promulgada en 2021

establece un cupo laboral mínimo del 1% para personas travestis, transexuales y transgénero en la administración pública nacional

.


En contra de la ley


Tanto el suyo como otros despidos en el sector público se dieron en un contexto de discriminación. “La despiden con tutela sindical, estaba de licencia médica y además había ingresado por el cupo laboral trans. Ser despedida en ese contexto se torna discriminatorio tanto por su actividad gremial como por su género. Además de que se encontraba de licencia médica”, explicó a

Presentes

 la abogada de Narmona, Eliana Bagnera, integrante del equipo jurídico de la Asociación de Trabajadores del Estado (ATE) Capital.


Según el último

registro disponible

 (enero de 2025), de les 150 trabajadores TTNB (travesti, trans y no binarie) despedides en el primer año de gestión del gobierno de Javier Milei, 50 fueron reincorporades. Treinta y tres lo hicieron por vía gremial …

author: anred
title: Salario Mínimo Vital y Móvil: Aumento por decreto de apenas 7200 pesos
content:
Tras el fracaso de la negociación entre empresarios y sindicatos, el Poder Ejecutivo estableció unilateralmente los nuevos valores del Salario Mínimo, Vital y Móvil (SMVyM). El piso será de 383.800 pesos en septiembre y llegará a 437.000 en abril del próximo año. De esta manera, el gobierno fijó un monto aún menor del que habían propuesto las cámaras empresarias y el Salario se mantiene muy por debajo de la línea de pobreza.

Por Red Eco Alternativo.


En la fallida reunión del Consejo del Salario, los empresarios habían propuesto para abril un sueldo de 468 mil pesos; en tanto los sindicatos, teniendo en cuenta que la canasta básica es de 1.564.716 de pesos, habían pedido que para diciembre de este año el salario llegara a 993 mil.


Ante la falta de acuerdo, el gobierno fijó de manera unilateral, a través de la Resolución 4/2026, que el salario mínimo pasará de 383.800 pesos en septiembre a 437.000 en abril.


Para los trabajadores jornalizados, el valor de la hora se incrementará de 1.919 a 2.185 pesos durante el mismo período.


El nuevo salario mínimo, mes a mes:

-Septiembre de 2026: $383.800 mensuales / $1.919 por hora.-Octubre de 2026: $391.200 mensuales / $1.956 por hora.-Noviembre de 2026: $398.800 mensuales / $1.994 por hora.-Diciembre de 2026: $406.400 mensuales / $2.032 por hora.-Enero de 2027: $414.200 mensuales / $2.071 por hora.-Febrero de 2027: $422.000 mensuales / $2.110 por hora.-Marzo de 2027: $429.600 mensuales / $2.148 por hora.-Abril de 2027: $437.000 mensuales / $2.185 por hora.

title: Shitegeist: Life in a World Designed to Fail - Sam Buchanan
content:

From AI to polluted beaches, things are increasingly shit. But as new shitscapes manifest, we should not be fooled into thinking this is brand new shit. This shit has been around for a long time and people have devised ways of resisting it. We are in danger of forgetting our anti-shit history leaving us at the mercy of both the insanely wealthy shit merchants who want to keep us isolated, unhappy and ignorant, and by the moderately prosperous who undermine any real challenge to the shitus quo, offering us a few wet wipes while building their own private sewer systems... Basically, this is an essay from Aotearoa/New Zealand on enshittification and what to do about it.

title: 24ωρη απεργία των εργαζομένων στη Vodafone – Παράσταση διαμαρτυρίας, Πέμπτη 10/09, στις 15.30, στις κ.ε. Vodafone, Χαλάνδρι
content:
Την Πέμπτη το σωματέιο εργαζομένων στη Vodafone καλεί σε 24ωρη απεργία, ενάντια στο νέο κύμα κατάργησης τμημάτων τηλεφωνικών κέντρων και στο καθεστώς εντατικοποιήσης που επιφέρει με τους εργαζομένους να καταλήγουν υποχρεωμένοι να δουλεύουν και στη σταθερή, και στη κινητή υποστήριξη με χαμηλές αμοιβές. Οι εργαζόμενοι απαιτούν να μπει τέλος στην εντατικοποίηση αυτή, οι εργαζόμενοι να εργάζονται πάνω σε ένα αντικείμενο εργασίας, να γίνουν αυξήσεις των μισθών και να υπογραφεί Συλλογική Σύμβαση Εργασίας. Το σωματείο καλεί παράλληλα σε παράσταση διαμαρτυρίας, την Πέμπτη 10/9, στις 15.30, στις κεντρικές εγκαταστάσεις της Vodafone.


Καλέσματα:


Σωματείο Εργαζομένων στη Vodafone


Όλοι στην 24ωρη απεργία την Πέμπτη 10 Σεπτέμβρη και στην παράσταση διαμαρτυρίας στο Χαλάνδρι την ίδια ημέρα στις 15.30 την ώρα που το ΔΣ του Σωματείου θα έχει συνάντηση με την εργοδοσία.


Συνάδελφοι,


Τους τελευταίους μήνες η εταιρεία υλοποιεί αυτό ακριβώς που είχε προαναγγείλει το προηγούμενο διάστημα και είχε ξεκινήσει με τις απολύσεις που είχαν γίνει μέσα στην άνοιξη. Στα τηλεφωνικά κέντρα αφού κατήργησε ολόκληρα τμήματα (Sam,SOHO PT κ.α) και έριξε τους συναδέλφους σε τμήματα με βάρδιες (1399,Combo Care) ήρθε η σειρά και άλλων τμημάτων να ολοκληρωθεί το λεγόμενο converge. Δηλαδή οι συνάδελφοι γίνονται λάστιχο και εξυπηρετούν κινητή μαζί με σταθερή ενώ και στα τμήματα της κινητής φορτώσανε στους Postpay και τα Prepay και αντίστροφα.


Η νέα δυστοπία που μας επιφυλάσσει η εταιρεία είναι οι κλήσεις να πέφτουν βροχή, να κάνει ένας εργαζόμενος τη δουλειά για δύο, να εναλλάσσει τις αρμοδιότητες, για να βγάζει η εταιρεία τα κέρδη της ελαχιστοποιώντας το κόστος και μετρώντας το κάθε λεπτό με βάση τους δείκτες αποδοτικότητας και ταυτόχρονα οι μισθοί να παραμένουν χαρτζιλίκι και να μην φτάνουν ούτε μέχρι τα μέσα του μήνα.


Εμείς σε αυτήν την νέα πραγματικότητα καλούμε τους συνάδελφους να βάλουν εκείνοι στοπ.


Να βάλουν τις ανάγκες τους μπροστά διεκδικώντας καλύτερους όρους εργασίας και αμοιβές χωρίς να περιμένουν κάθε μήνα να δούνε αν θα πιάσουν το μπόνους που και σε αυτό έχει πέσει κούρεμα αποδεικνύοντας ότι η εταιρεία το χρησιμοποιεί κατά το δοκούν.


Στόχος είναι ο αγώνας μας να συνδεθεί με τον αγώνα για την υπογραφή Συλλογικής Σύμβασης Εργασίας στην Vodafone και να μεγαλώσει η διεκδίκηση και στα υπόλοιπα τμήματα της εταιρείας.


Οι κινητοποιήσεις μέσα στο καλοκαίρι έστειλαν ηχηρό μήνυμα στην εργοδοσία ότι οι εργαζόμενοι του TSR και των τηλεφωνικών κέντρων θα συνεχίζουν να παλεύουν και να διεκδικούν καλυτέρους όρους εργασίας απέναντι στην εντατικοποίηση και στο πλάνο της εταιρείας να μας κάνει «εργαζόμενους μπαλαντέρ» .


Η χθεσινή μαζική συνέλευση έδειξε ότι οι συνάδελφοι είναι διατεθειμένοι να το πάνε μέχρι τέρμα συνεχίζοντας την κλιμάκωση του αγώνα με 24ωρη απεργία την Πέμπτη 10 Σεπτέμβρη και παράσταση διαμαρτυρίας στο Χαλάνδρι την ίδια ημέρα στις 15.30, την ώρα που το ΔΣ του Σωματείου θα έχει συνάντηση με την εργοδοσία.


Στην περίπτωση που η εργοδοσία δεν δεχθεί τα αιτήματα μας οι κινητοποιήσεις θα συνεχιστούν με περαιτέρω κλιμάκωση και αυτό είναι κάτι που προκύπτει μέσα από τις συνελεύσεις και δείχνει την αποφασιστικότητα που υπάρχει και το τι μπορούμε να κάνουμε όταν συσπειρωνόμαστε και διεκδικούμε οργανωμένα.


Χαρακτηριστικό είναι πως στην χθεσινή συνέλευση δόθηκε η οδηγία από τους από πάνω να κλείσει το chat του τεχνικού της σταθερής για τις ώρες της συνέλευσης προκειμένου να μην πέφτουν τα chat ενώ επιστρατευτήκαν και συνάδελφοι από τα τμήματα του Retention για να κάνουν καταγραφές των κλήσεων καθώς οι αναμονές είχαν πιάσει ταβάνι.


Καλούμε τα τμήματα του τηλεφωνικού κέντρου και τις διευθύνσεις Retention & Sales σε συμμετοχή στην απεργία καθώς και τους συναδέλφους στην υπόλοιπη εταιρεία να στηρίξουν με την συμμετοχή τους τον αγώνα μας καθώς ο παρονομαστής είναι κοινός και η εκμετάλλευση αλλάζει μορφή.


Να μαζικοποιηθεί ο αγώνας μας για να αρχίσει η εργοδοσία τις διαπραγματεύσεις με το Σωματείο μας για την υπογραφή Συλλογικής Συμβάσης Εργασίας στη Vodafone όπου θα κατοχυρώνει σύγχρονα δικαιώματα, αξιοπρεπείς μισθούς και σταθερό εργάσιμο χρόνο για όλους τους εργαζόμενους κόντρα στις ατομικές συμβάσεις εργασίας που υπογράφουμε σήμερα.


Να γίνουν προσλήψεις προσωπικού στα υποστελεχωμένα τμήματα κόντρα στην λογική των συγχωνεύσεων και του υπαλλήλου μπαλαντέρ που θα εξυπηρετεί τα πάντα.


Διεκδικούμε:


– Κάθε εργαζόμενος να δουλεύει αποκλειστικά σε ένα αντικείμενο εργασίας. Είτε υποστήριξη στη σταθερή είτε στη κινητή.


– Αυξήσεις στους …

title: Worker-owned bookstore opened in Asheville, 2008
content:
Firestorm Books & Coffee () opened in Asheville, North Carolina in 2008 as a worker-owned, self-managed bookstore and coffee shop. The collective runs without bosses or supervisors, making decisions through horizontal consensus, and stocks titles from AK Press, PM Press, Chelsea Green, Feral House, Autonomedia and more. Since 2014, they've operated out of a storefront on Haywood Road in West Asheville, hosting events, workshops, film screenings and fundraisers alongside organic coffee and vegan pastries.

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: Labor Day and the Fight for Women’s Freedom
content:
Labor Day is a time to recognize the workers who built this country, and the movements that fought to make work more fair, safe, and dignified. For women, the labor movement has always been about more than a paycheck. It has been about having the freedom to build a life on our own terms.

From the women who organized for better wages and safer working conditions to the feminists who demanded—and still demand— equal pay, paid leave, and an end to workplace discrimination, generations of women have fought for economic independence as a fundamental part of equality.

Yet more than a century of organizing has not erased the inequalities women face at work. Women working full-time, year-round earn about 81 cents for every dollar earned by men. The gap is even wider for many women of color: compared with white, non-Hispanic men, Black women earn about 69 cents and Hispanic women about 57 cents for every dollar. Black and Hispanic women also face the compounding effects of occupational segregation, with women of color disproportionately represented in lower-paying jobs. In 2023 alone, the Department of Labor estimated that Black women lost $42.7 billion and Hispanic women lost $53.3 billion in wages compared with white men because of occupational and industry segregation.

Women remain underrepresented in positions of power and leadership. Women hold just 10.4% of Fortune 500 CEO positions, while women of color make up only 7.8% of Fortune 500 board members. Equality at work cannot simply mean having the opportunity to enter the workforce. It must also mean having an equal opportunity to advance and build economic security.

That fight has always extended beyond the workplace. Women’s economic freedom is inseparable from the freedom to make decisions about our own bodies, families, and futures. Without reproductive freedom, economic independence is limited. The cost of an abortion can include the cost of the procedure itself, but also transportation, childcare, time away from work, and other expenses.

For women entering the workforce, bodily autonomy is more than an abstract idea. It can determine whether someone can finish school, accept a job, move to a new city, pursue a career, or decide when and whether to become a parent.

In fact, 45% of 18-34 year old workers would reject a job offer in a state where abortion is illegal and 62% would “probably not” or “definitely not” live in a state that banned abortion at all. As of July 2026, only 53.8% of young people were employed. In an increasingly difficult job market, young people should not have to choose between economic opportunity and control over their own bodies.

The feminist movement has understood this connection for generations. The fight for women’s equality has never been limited to any single workplace, policy, or election. It has been a fight for the freedom to participate fully in society and to make decisions about our own lives. That is the promise behind the Equal Rights Amendment, which Congress must recognize.

As the 2026 midterm elections get underway, voters have an opportunity to decide what kind of freedom women will have in the years ahead. The issues on the ballot, from wages and workplace protections to reproductive rights are deeply connected.

Women demand freedom. We demand the freedom to work, earn, organize, vote, choose, and to determine the course of our own lives. That has always been the promise of the feminist movement and this Labor Day, it is still the fight ahead.

author: Unknown
title: Bingöl'de KHK'lilerden çağrı: İhraçlar görevlerine iade edilsin
content:
Bingöl – Eğitim ve Bilim Emekçileri Sendikası (Eğitim-Sen) Bingöl Şubesi öncülüğünde Kanun Hükmünde Kararname (KHK) ile ihraç edilen kamu emekçileri için Kent Meydanı’nda açıklama yapıldı. Açıklamaya KHK’liler ve Demokratik Kurumlar Platformu temsilcileri de katıldı. "Hakikatler ihraç edilemez" ve "KHK’liler onurumuzdur" yazılı pankartlar ardından konuşan KHK’li öğretmen Mursel Bek, işlerini iyi yaptıkları için ihraç edildiklerini ifade ederek 10 yıldır sürdürdükleri mücadeleden vazgeçmeyeceklerini belirtti.

Bek’in ardından açıklama metnini okuyan KHK’li öğretmen İsmail Koç, 15 Temmuz darbe girişiminin ardından ilan edilen OHAL’in kısa sürede muhalif kamu emekçilerini tasfiye etmenin aracına dönüştüğünü söyledi. On binlerce kamu emekçisinin etkili bir soruşturma ve savunma hakkı tanınmadan ihraç edildiğini kaydeden Koç, insanlık dışı koşullarla baş başa bırakıldıklarını ifade etti. Sürecin bürokrasiye kurban edildiğini dile getiren Koç, 23 Ocak 2017’de kurulan OHAL İşlemleri İnceleme Komisyonu’nun emekçileri yıllarca beklettiğini ve kapandığı 22 Ocak 2023 tarihine kadar başvuruların büyük çoğunluğunu reddettiğini aktardı. KESK’li ihraçların önemli bir kısmında hukuki mücadelesinin hala sürdüğünü ekleyen Koç, bu mücadelenin sadece bireysel bir hak arayışı olmadığını, yürütülen direnişin hukukun üstünlüğü ve demokratik bir ülkenin geleceği için yapıldığını ifade etti. Türkiye’nin kronik sorunlarının çatışmayla değil barış, demokrasi ve eşitlik temelinde çözülebileceğini, KHK mağduriyetlerinin giderilmesinin de toplumsal barışın en önemli adımlarından biri olacağını belirtti.

Koç, açıklamanın sonunda hükümete seslenerek taleplerini şöyle sıraladı: “Mahkemeler üzerindeki siyasi baskılara son verilmesini, yargı süreçlerinin hızlandırılmasını, bekletilen dosyaların derhal sonuçlandırılmasını ve hakkında beraat, takipsizlik veya göreve dönüş kararı bulunan tüm kamu emekçilerinin derhal görevlerine iade edilmesini istiyoruz.”

Açıklama, atılan sloganlarının ardından sona erdi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Luis Feliz Leon
title: Persecuted by Trump, Will Unions Build Towards May 2028?
content:
Three years ago the United Auto Workers, glowing with confidence after a successful strike at the Big 3 and pledging ambitious new organizing drives, put out a call for a national strike on May 1, 2028.


UAW President Shawn Fain called for unions to align their contracts with the Big 3 to build leverage and create a crisis for the billionaire class. It was a new day in the UAW, and a wider labor renewal felt possible.


May 2028 is now only a year and a half away. Are unions getting in gear for a

season of strikes

and labor action around then, as contracts expire in manufacturing, education, logistics, grocery, and the building trades?


Some are. Labor Notes has found 830,000 workers with contracts planned or expected to expire from March to July 2028

(see illustration below)

.


These include 150,000 auto workers at the Big 3, 153,000 Postal Workers (APWU), though they are unlikely to strike, 95,000 grocery workers with the Food and Commercial Workers Union (UFCW), and 77,000 K-12 educators with the California Teachers Association.


“Together, we can turn May Day into a national day of reckoning,” Fain

wrote

 last year, taking stock of the progress towards this goal. “If more union workers stand up together, we will all have more power to win what we’re owed.”


FIGHTING ON NEW TERRAIN


What we are owed has been growing, amid Trump’s

 extreme attacks

 on workers and unions.


Notable contract expirations in 2028.


One million federal workers have

lost their right

 to collective bargaining. The National Labor Relations Board and

other federal agencies

 meant to protect workers have been

left unable

to fulfill their essential roles. Tens of thousands of immigrant workers, including union members, have been stripped of their

legal status

 and rights, subjected to

criminalization

 and

detention

.


May Day 2028 wasn’t initially about fighting Trump’s billionaire power grab. But since Trump took office, the terrain has shifted. Mass protests have become more frequent, and more urgently needed to stem the volley of attacks on workers and on democratic elections.


Massive weekend protests

 that drew millions, organized by Indivisible and No Kings, haven’t been able to reverse Trump’s attacks, though they are important training grounds to welcome new activists.  (

Bring your union banner

!) The next big one, “

No Kings: Vote Early

,” is scheduled for October 17. It will include block parties, rallies, and walks to the polls.


But the lessons from these mobilizations have started to shift tactics to include large economic disruptions. Today’s resistance movement recognizes that

one-off weekend

 protests aren’t enough.


Unions are powerful members of a resistance coalition not only because they are robust voter turnout operations, but more importantly because they can channel the structural power of workers in key industries to grind the system to a halt.


In January, when Trump sent a swarm of federal agents into the Twin Cities on a rampage, he lit a match to the tinder that unions and community groups had been laying through decades of coalition work. People’s resistance spread into school walkouts, sit-ins, demonstrations, and strikes.


“We modeled our ‘ICE Out’ work similarly to how we prepare to go on strike—leaders in each building and regional leads who work together to cover the city,” said St. Paul educator Mara Solis. “Each school had parent captains to work with our educator captains.”


These escalating actions grew into a mass uprising that nearly shut down a large metro area. Federal agents beat a retreat from the terror spectacles in Twin Cities streets after January 23, when at least 100,000 people

marched

 through downtown Minneapolis and nearly 1 million across the state skipped work to

participate

 in a massive political strike, including nonunion construction workers and restaurant workers who called out from popular downtown venues and supermarkets.


It showed how, when unions act like movement organizations, nonunion workers can join them in common cause, which is necessary in a country where 90 percent of the population working for a private-sector employer earns a living in a nonunion workplace.


If the Twin Cities offered an example of layer after layer of society erupting into open rebellion, how can that be replicated nationally? We already have a rendezvous date for massive economic disruption, in the months leading up to the next presidential election …

author: Gladys Stagno
title: Batacazo de la ultraderecha: “Alemania está viviendo su crisis política más profunda de las últimas décadas”
content:
El triunfo de Alternativa para Alemania (AfD) con casi el 44% de los votos en Sajonia-Anhalt sacudió el escenario político y profundizó la crisis de los partidos tradicionales. “Estamos viendo un parteaguas”, advierte el sociólogo alemán Torge Löding.


La cúpula de la AfD celebra el triunfo en Sajonia-Anhalt (Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance)


Por Gladys Stagno


“Lo que pasó en el estado de Sajonia-Anhalt es algo que podríamos llamar un terremoto político”. La expresión es de Torge Löding, periodista y sociólogo alemán, quien describe así el triunfo de la ultraderechista Alternativa para Alemania (AfD) el domingo pasado en uno de los 16 estados federados de Alemania.


Si bien se trata de uno de los estados más pequeños en cuanto a peso económico y poblacional, el batacazo que le dio a AfD el 43,8% de los votos —frente al 17,2% de la oficialista Unión Demócrata Cristiana (CDU)— no sólo cambia el juego democrático establecido en ese país desde 1945, sino que abre la puerta a que lo mismo ocurra a nivel nacional.


“Es la primera vez que un partido de extrema derecha, después de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, está cerca de crear gobierno. La mal llamada Alternativa para Alemania, porque no dignifican una alternativa para este país, no logra tener la mayoría absoluta, pero logra cerca del 45%. El mejor resultado que cualquier partido obtuvo en una elección en los últimos diez años en Alemania”, asegura Löding, jefe de la oficina regional de la Fundación Rosa Luxemburgo en Buenos Aires, en diálogo con Canal Abierto.


Por su parte, la socialdemocracia (SPD) obtuvo el 9,2%, los Verdes (Grüne) el 8,9%, la Izquierda (Die Linke) el 8,5%, y la Alianza Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW) el 5,2%. Según el sistema alemán, sólo los partidos que obtienen un mínimo del 5% tienen representación en el Landtag (Parlamento).


Con estos números, AfD obtendría 39 escaños. Para formar gobierno, se necesitan 42.


Racismo y federalización


En este escenario, la preocupación que expresa Löding es por partida doble: por la agenda racista, que enarbola AfD, y por su proyección nacional.


“Su propuesta excluye gente profesional que no es de origen alemán de la vida laboral. En la agenda cultural, quiere terminar con la escuela pública y eliminar esa posibilidad para la gente que no nació en Alemania. También tiene una agenda vinculada con la reemigración, que significa que no importa qué pasaporte tengas: si no tienes sangre alemana te pueden deportar”, explica.


En lo económico, detalla que el partido ganador “tiene una agenda ultraneoliberal, parecida a la de Javier Milei, pero se vincula con garantías sociales sólo para alemanes de sangre alemana”.


En cuanto a las implicancias federales, el triunfo encabezado por Ulrich Seigmund, candidato de la AfD, desató una crisis política en la cúpula del gobierno alemán, donde los democristianos pasaron de 40 a 16 escaños. El propio canciller Friedrich Merz manifestó: “Debo admitir que esta es la derrota electoral más devastadora que ha sufrido la CDU en años, incluso décadas”. Luego admitió que estas elecciones “han cambiado no solo Sajonia-Anhalt, sino toda Alemania” y advirtió que el resultado tendrá también repercusiones internacionales.


Por su parte, la líder nacional de AfD, Alice Weidel, se subió al resultado y aprovechó para reclamar un cambio en el rumbo político y pedir la convocatoria a unas nuevas elecciones federales.


“Esta elección tiene un impacto a nivel nacional, está temblando el gobierno de Merz y yo creo que no va a sobrevivir a este mes. Es una crisis profunda que podría llevar en el corto plazo a nuevas elecciones a nivel federal ahogado por la elección en un estado que es tal vez es el menos importante”, resume Löding.


Y agrega: “Alemania está viviendo su crisis política más profunda de las últimas décadas, y estamos viendo con este resultado un parteaguas. Todo el espectro de partidos democráticos se está quedando corto. No logran ni todos juntos crear una mayoría para después votar un primer ministro de alguno de los partidos democráticos”.


El miedo a la guerra


Puesto a explicar el por qué de la crisis, Löding sostiene que se trata de una reacción a la crisis económica: “El encarecimiento de los combustibles, de los alimentos, de la vida en general producto de la guerra de Ucrania y Rusia y las guerras de Trump llevan a una situación complicada a Alemania. Y la gente está harta, decepcionada, buscando salida. Obviamente creo que votar un partido nazi nunca puede ser …

author: Unknown
title: Cartographie des extrêmes droites du Grésivaudan
content:
«

 

Située entre Grenoble et Chambéry, la vallée du Grésivaudan est encadrée par les massifs de Chartreuse et de Belledonne. La communauté de communes regroupe 43 communes. Creuset d'industries pionnières, le Grésivaudan reste une terre d'innovation accueillant aujourd'hui des activités industrielles de pointe qui en font l'un des pôles d'excellence économique de l‘Isère. La qualité de vie offerte par son environnement naturel et la diversité de ses activités lui confèrent une forte attractivité. Bienvenue dans le Grésivaudan

 

!

 

»


Office du tourisme Belledonne Chartreuse


Mais, derrière cette vision idyllique, le Grésivaudan est, comme le reste du département de l'Isère, gangrené par la présence de plus en plus inquiétante des réseaux de l'extrême-droite.


Il y a d'un côté les résultats électoraux du Rassemblement national ou de Reconquête. Une masse d'électeurs glisse vers des partis fascisants sans avoir le moindre scrupule.


Les réseaux des catholiques intégristes, en toute discrétion, s'implantent grâce à leurs diverses associations. Leur objectif est d'imposer leurs visions rétrogrades et de contrôler la jeunesse.

author: Maira Escardovelli
title: Espionado por Mendonça em 2020, professor vê “natureza golpista” em atuação de ministro
content:
“Escândalo de natureza golpista” é como o antropólogo, cientista político, escritor e ex-secretário Nacional de Segurança Pública Luiz Eduardo Soares traduz o momento de crise institucional no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF). A Corte monopoliza as atenções da opinião pública desde que o

ministro André Mendonça

 retirou, no dia 1° de setembro, o sigilo do relatório da Polícia Federal (PF) com mensagens trocadas entre o ex-banqueiro do Master, Daniel Vorcaro, e o ministro Alexandre de Moraes. Na avaliação de Soares, que ocupou o cargo no Ministério da Justiça  no primeiro mandato de Lula como presidente, Mendonça está usando suas prerrogativas para interferir no pleito eleitoral. 


“O timing de cada vazamento selecionado, de cada suspensão de sigilo, promovendo a disseminação de indícios que se convertem imediatamente em condenações, afetam e inclinam a opinião pública. O problema não é cada decisão em si mesma, mas o timing preciso de sua divulgação, produzindo uma narrativa com potencial explosivo, politicamente.

Trata-se da instrumentalização institucional com propósito criminoso de incidir na dinâmica política numa conjuntura que se aproxima do momento do voto, momento que não é fugaz, que gera efeitos irreversíveis”

, explica Soares.


Professor aposentado do Instituto de Ciências Sociais da Universidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro (UERJ), Soares foi alvo da gestão de André Mendonça no Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública (MJSP), no governo do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, hoje preso por tentativa de golpe de Estado. Em 2020, ele foi um dos três professores universitários alvos de dossiês produzidos pela antiga Secretaria de Operações Integradas (Seopi) do MJSP, à época chefiada por Mendonça, como revelado

pelo jornalista Rubens Valente no portal UOL

.


Além de três docentes, o documento listou mais de 570 servidores federais e estaduais que foram monitorados pela pasta. Todos os nomes eram críticos ao governo de Jair Bolsonaro e foram identificados como integrantes do movimento político antifascista. 


“As semanas que se seguiram [após a divulgação do dossiê na imprensa] foram angustiantes, porque começaram a pipocar nas redes sociais agressões e ameaças com linguagem fascista.

 Era impossível saber se as fontes das hostilidades estavam situadas no governo federal ou eram robôs, simulando participação espontânea de militantes bolsonaristas”, relembra Soares. 


A

Agência Pública

 teve acesso a um dos relatórios produzidos pelo Ministério da Justiça, na época, contra o movimento Policiais Antifascismo. O grupo divulgou em 2016 um manifesto de repúdio ao impeachment contra a ex-presidenta Dilma Rousseff e em 2020 manifestaram apoio aos movimentos antifascistas contra o  então presidente da República, Jair Bolsonaro. 


Por que isso importa?


Os dossiês criados na gestão de André Mendonça no Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública durante o governo de Jair Bolsonaro foram considerados inconstitucionais pelo STF em 2022.

A relatora do processo, ministra Cármen Lúcia chegou a equipar a produção do dossiê às atividades realizadas durante a ditadura militar brasileira.


O relatório, que contém fotos e a identificação de nomes de líderes do grupo, afirma que “o ANTIFA representa grupos que internacionalmente lutam contra o fascismo e o autoritarismo. A ação Antifascista Brasil, ou Antifas, é um movimento descentralizado, de ideologia esquerda, abarcando ideais do comunismo, anarquismo e sindicalismo, que tem como reivindicações autodeclaradas o combate ao racismo, fascismo, autoritarismo, machismo, homofobia e violência policial. Se declaram defensores das liberdades democráticas e direitos das minorias”. 


Em seguida, são apresentadas diversas manifestações com participação do grupo. “Diante dos acontecimentos expostos cronologicamente, podendo, nesta breve análise, não ter sido referenciado algum outro evento,

frisa-se que esta pasta vem acompanhando, desde o dia 24ABR2020, o movimento denominado Policiais Antifascistas que envolve ao menos 17 (dezessete) estados, em que policiais ou agentes públicos ligados à segurança pública posicionam-se em favor desta causa

 através de redes sociais como Facebook, Instagram, Twitter e YouTube”, afirma o relatório. 


Identificado e monitorado no dossiê, Abdael Ambruster, policial e diretor do Sindicato dos Policiais Penais de São Paulo (Sinppenal), e integrantes do movimento Policiais Antifascistas protocolaram uma notícia-crime contra André Mendonça por …

author: By Ryan Fatica and Hannah Kass, Contributors
title: Treesit Blocks US-Mexico Border Wall Construction for Six Weeks in Arizona
content:
Santa Cruz County, AZ – On a cool, cloudy morning in the San Rafael Valley in Southern Arizona, a young person popped their head over the edge of a platform in a tree, perched fifty feet above the rolling prairieland below. “Hi! Thanks for coming!” they shouted down to the group of newcomers approaching the ancient cottonwood tree they now live in. When asked how they’re doing up there, they reported feeling calm and that they had everything they need. “I do miss hugs,” they said.


Since July 27, land defenders have been living in the ancient cottonwood trees they affectionately call “Grandmothers” along the U.S.-Mexico border near the old townsite of Lochiel, Arizona, 85 miles south of Tucson. The trees are estimated to be over 200 years old. 


For over a month, the land defenders have been preventing the construction of two 30-foot-tall steel-and-concrete bollard walls construction companies contracted by the Trump administration are building along Arizona’s southern border. Construction has been halted along a three-mile stretch or borderland. Although many parts of the border have a “primary” bollard wall that was constructed during the first Trump administration, only a shoddy, collapsing fence marks the boundary between the U.S. and Mexico south of Lochiel. Here, construction crews had been building both walls at once. 


On the day the treesit began, employees of Fisher Sand and Gravel, the private contractors that won

the $352.49 million contract

 from the Department of Homeland Security to construct the secondary border wall, cut down three ancient cottonwood trees. In response, one protester stood in the way of construction work to prevent the destruction of another ancient cottonwood. He was

briefly arrested

 by Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Deputies before being released twelve hours later without charges. 


A mature mesquite tree on the southern side of the “primary” border wall (Photo: Ryan Fatica)


The action galvanized dozens of land defenders to flock to the area and establish a treesit, where defenders rotate their presence in shifts. 


Leah, a protester who helped establish the treesit, told Unicorn Riot that a small handful of people set up the platform in the middle of the night, under a bright, nearly full moon. At first, Leah said, they had some trouble getting the treesit platform–made of rectangular plywood reinforced by 2 x 4s–rigged into the tree. They also had to work around a hive of bees that called the tree  home. Eventually, by around 4 a.m., the treesit was established. Setting up the treesit “felt almost like a game in a funny way,” said Leah. 


Since that night, supporters have established an encampment around the Grandmother tree, which Kate Scott, co-founder of the Madrean Archipelago Wildlife Center calls “Hope Zone” or “Esperanza Zone.” 


In the zone, campers sleep, cook for each other, sing and play music, and experiment with a new way of being together in this expanse of savannah known as the San Rafael Valley. The camp “gives people a chance to say what they want to say and share what they want to share, and meld it into what we all co-create together,” said Scott. “It’s a non-hierarchical camp … we’re all leaders.” 


When asked how it feels to him to be at camp, Miguel, a tree-sitter who spent several weeks there, some of it perched high in the cottonwood, said “One of the best words I can use to describe the feeling there is love. People have so much love for the land and for the people resisting–a lot of care and solidarity.” Miguel said his family came to the U.S. from Mexico in the 1980s, when crossing the border was much simpler. “These sorts of issues feel very personal to me,” Miguel said. 


Tents set up in an open pasture north of the U.S.-Mexico border host land defenders committed to protecting the cottonwoods and defending the tree sit. Photo contributed by Ryan Fatica

.


The two parallel walls will be built

using “Smart Wall” technology

 – AI-powered camera surveillance, bright lights, and detection devices, coupled with the double-border “enforcement zone” design. The contract for this double border wall is one of 34 Smart Wall projects comprising new border wall construction funded by billions of dollars allocated from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act for militarized border construction. 


Lochiel is an old town site in the San Rafael Valley, which serves as a critical ecosystem, home to one of the most important wildlife corridors in the …

title: Elezioni in Sassonia-Anhalt: una lettura del risultato ottenuto da Afd
content:
Il partito di ultradestra guidato da Alice Weidel ha ottenuto oltre il 44% dei voti nel land della Sassonia-Anhalt alle ultime elezioni. 


Questo risultato va letto secondo una serie di aspetti che compongono un quadro di tendenza generale, seppur con delle specificità date dal contesto tedesco e del territorio. Inoltre, va analizzato il processo storico in cui si è determinato un consenso così schiacciante nei confronti di un’opzione reazionaria e xenofoba come questa. La crisi sociale ed economica che investe la Germania e più in generale l’Europa, la guerra e la corsa al riarmo, i rapporti con gli USA e con la Russia sono tutti elementi significativi. Al contempo le contraddizioni di questo partito sono forti e potranno rappresentare uno spazio di possibilità per una contrapposizione dal basso? 


Insieme a Nicola Carella, compagno che da tempo vive a Berlino abbiamo affrontato questi temi per comprendere quanto accaduto.

One of the enigmas of the second Trump administration is that the grassroots fascist activity of 2017 to 2020

The above illustration appears courtesy of

Chris Veal

. You can support Spider-Man in his efforts to resist fascism

.

demonstrations

Nonetheless, neo-Nazis like Jake Lang are testing the waters, hoping to revitalize mass far-right street politics, while groups like the Proud Boys have once more taken to

up

launched

speaking

At the same time, they will claim that the Trump administration has not gone far enough, and will attempt to promote and normalize vigilante violence—which could be especially dangerous at a time when the state is providing cover for fascist terror. As the Trump era

nears its end

title: Die Stille nach dem Zusammenstoß- zur Situation von Henry aus dem Antifa-Ost-Verfahren
content:
Es war ein sonniger Dienstag im August, wir saßen zusammen, nach einem weiteren von über 50 Prozesstagen im Dresdner Antifa-Ost-Verfahren und Thema war auch Henry A. Er war an diesem Tag nicht zum Prozess erschienen, denn wegen akuter Suizidalität war er in eine Psychiatrie eingewiesen worden. Vier Tage später sollte er von einer S-Bahn überrollt werden.


Henry A. – seit langer Zeit im Visier des sächsischen Staatsschutzes


Henry war seit

2013 im Visier

 der sächsischen Repressionsbehörden. Im Zusammenhang mit Ermittlungen gegen die Fanszene der BSG Chemie Leipzig wurde über Jahre gegen ihn wegen des Verdachts der Bildung einer kriminellen Vereinigung nach

§ 129 StGB

 ermittelt. Seine Telefone wurden monatelang überwacht, er wurde observiert und seine Bewegungen und Kontakte wurden erfasst. Dabei wurden auch Gespräche mit Journalist, Ärzt und Anwält aufgezeichnet. 2016 wurde das Verfahren eingestellt; der sächsische Datenschutzbeauftragte beanstandete später unter anderem den Umgang der Ermittlungsbehörden mit der Überwachung und der dabei erfassten geschützten Kommunikation: „Im Sommer 2018 habe ich nach alledem das Landeskriminalamt wegen der Verletzung seiner Mitwirkungspflichten bei der Einhaltung von Verfahrensregelungen im Rahmen von Maßnahmen der Telekommunikationsüberwachung (TKÜ) nach § 100a StPO gemäß § 29 Absatz 1 SächsDSG gegenüber dem Sächsischen Staatsministerium des Innern förmlich beanstandet. Ebenso erging eine Beanstandung der Staatsanwaltschaft Dresden wegen Verstößen gegen die gesetzliche Pflicht, Aufzeichnungen von Kommunikation aus dem Kernbereich privater Lebensgestaltung bzw. mit besonders geschützten Berufsgeheimnisträgern unverzüglich zu löschen, gegenüber dem Sächsischen Staatsministerium der Justiz“, so der Landesdatenschutzbeauftragte in seinem Tätigkeitsbericht von 2017/18 (als

PDF

, a.a.O. S. 26 ff)


Doch damit endete die staatliche Verfolgung Henrys nicht. Aus dem ursprünglichen Verfahren gingen weitere Ermittlungen hervor, auch diese wurden wieder eingestellt. 2021 wurde seine Wohnung erneut durchsucht, zunächst wegen des Verdachts der Beteiligung an einem Angriff auf rechte Fußballfans, später wegen eines Betäubungsmittelverdachts. Eine Durchsuchung dauerte rund 14 Stunden, und hinterlässt eine verwüstete Wohung, eine weitere dauerte mehrere Stunden. Belastbare Belege für die jeweils erhobenen Vorwürfe fanden sich nie; zu einer Anklage kam es auch hier nicht.


Auffällig ist dabei LKA-Ermittler Patrick H., der bereits an der Überwachung Henrys im Verfahren ab 2013 beteiligt war. Er tauchte später im Zusammenhang mit der Soko LinX wieder auf. So zieht sich die staatliche Verfolgung durch über ein Jahrzehnt. Und immer wieder geriet Henry ins Visier, es wurden Verfahren eingeleitet, er und sein Umfeld überwacht, die Wohnung durchsucht und schlussendlich eingestellt. Als er 2025 im

Antifa-Ost-Verfahren angeklagt

 wurde, wer er bereits mehr als zwölf Jahre staatlicher Ermittlungen ausgesetzt.


Der Verdacht, dass Polizeibeamt:innen persönliche Informationen über Henry an das rechtsextreme Magazin Compact

weitergereicht haben

, konnten letztendlich nicht bewiesen werden. Immer wieder versuchte Henry damals sich das Leben zu nehmen.


Henry vor dem OLG Dresden- 50 Prozesstage und kein Ende!


Henry saß nicht in Untersuchungshaft, sondern kam seit über 50 anstrengenden Prozesstagen zuverlässig zur Verhandlung. Seine Anwält:innen hatten versucht das OLG dazu zu bewegen an bestimmten Prozesstagen schon etwas früher aufzuhören, damit Henry an einer notwendigen Therapie hätte teilnehmen können. Der Senat lehnte dies mit der Begründung ab, es gelte das Beschleunigungsgebot, da andere Angeklagte in Untersuchungshaft säßen. Es komme auch nicht darauf an, dass die Mitangeklagten ausdrücklich erklärt hatten, mit dem früheren Schluss der Verhandlungstage einverstanden zu sein, denn das Beschleunigungsgebot stehe nicht zu deren Disposition.


Im Juli wird Henry in eine geschlossene Psychiatrie eingewiesen wegen akuter Selbstgefährdung, es folgt kurze Zeit später ein Selbsttötungsversuch.
